Commentary of al-Tha'labi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 22, verses 1–7:

Makkiyya, except six verses which were revealed in Madina, namely His saying ﴿These are two adversaries who dispute concerning their Lord﴾ up to ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾. It has 5,095 letters, 1,271 words [In the second copy: 1,270 words], and 78 verses.

Abu al-Hasan [In the second copy an addition: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan] al-Jurjani informed us more than once, saying: Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Isma'ili and Abu al-Shaykh Abdullah ibn Muhammad al-Asbahani informed us, both saying: Abu Ishaq Ibrahim ibn Sharik narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn Yunus al-Yarbu'i narrated to us, saying: Sallam ibn Sulaym al-Madaini narrated to us, saying: Harun ibn Kathir narrated to us, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, from Abu Umama, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Surat al-Hajj will be given the reward of a Hajj he performed and an 'Umra he performed, equal to the number of those who performed Hajj and 'Umra in the past and in the future" [1] [[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 7/123.]].

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord. Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing.﴾ Zilzala and zilzal: intense movement in a terrifying state, from the saying "his foot slipped" when it moved quickly from its place, then it was intensified.

﴿The Day you see it﴾

Meaning the Hour.

﴿Every nursing mother will forget﴾

That is, will be preoccupied, according to Ibn Abbas. al-Dahhak said: will be heedless. Ibn Hayyan said: will forget. It is said: "dhahila 'an kadha" meaning he left it and became occupied with something else, "adhhala, yadhulu dhuhulan," and "adhhalani al-shay' idhhalan." The poet said:

"Ṣaḥā qalbuhu yā ʿizz aw kād yadhhal"

﴿every nursing mother﴾

Meaning one who has a nursing child. Murdi'a is the woman who has a child she nurses for another; this is the view of the people of Kufa. The people of Basra said: it is said "imra'a mursi'" when it is intended as a descriptive attribute, like muqrib, mushriq, hamil and ha'id; when they intend the act, they add the ta' marbuta, so one says "murdi'a," the one who nurses her child.

﴿and every pregnant one will drop her load﴾

That is, will cast off her offspring from the terror of that Day.

﴿And you see people as drunkards, but they are not drunkards.﴾

al-Hasan [In the second copy: al-Husayn] said: its meaning: "and you see people as drunkards" from fear, "but they are not drunkards" from wine.

The people of meaning (ahl al-ma'ani) said: its figurative sense is "and you see people as if they were drunkards," supported by the reading of Abu Zur'a ibn 'Amr ibn Jarir: "wa-turā al-nās" with a dammed ta', meaning "they are thought to be."

The people of Kufa, except 'Asim, read "sukra" and "ma hum bi-sukra" without alif in both, and both are two dialects for the plural of drunkard, like kusala and kasala.

﴿But the punishment of Allah is severe.﴾

ʿImran ibn Husayn, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and others narrated that these two verses were revealed at night during the expedition of Bani al-Mustaliq, who were a tribe of Khuza'a, while the people were traveling. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called out, so they urged their mounts until they were around the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he recited them to them. No one wept more than on that night. When they woke in the morning, they did not unsaddle the beasts, did not pitch the tents, and did not cook any pot, while people were among weeping, bare-headed, sorrowful and pensive. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them [In the second copy an addition: "Do you know which day that is?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "That is the day when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will say to Adam: 'Arise and send forth the company of the Fire from your offspring.' Adam will say: 'From every how many?' Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will say: 'From every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine to the Fire and one to Paradise.' This was heavy upon the Muslims, and they wept and said: 'Then who will be saved, O Messenger of Allah?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said.]: "Rejoice, be steadfast and be near to the mark, for with you are two creatures which have never been in any people without multiplying them: Gog and Magog."

Then he said: "Indeed I hope you will be a quarter of the people of Paradise," so they proclaimed takbir and praised Allah. Then he said: "Indeed I hope you will be a third of the people of Paradise," so they proclaimed takbir and praised Allah. Then he said: "Indeed I hope you will be half of the people of Paradise," so they proclaimed takbir and praised Allah. Then he said: "Indeed I hope you will be two-thirds of the people of Paradise. The people of Paradise are one hundred and twenty rows, eighty of them are my community, and the Muslims among the disbelievers are not but like a mole on the flank of a camel or a spot on the foreleg of a beast, rather like a black hair on a white bull or a white hair on a black bull." Then he said: "And seventy thousand of my community will enter Paradise without reckoning." 'Umar said: "Seventy thousand?" He said: "Yes, and with each one seventy thousand." Then 'Ukasha ibn Mihsan stood up and said: "O Messenger of Allah, pray to Allah that He make me one of them." He said: "You are one of them." Then a man from the Ansar stood up and said: "Pray to Allah that He make me one of them." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "'Ukasha has outstripped you with it" [2].

﴿And among mankind is one who argues about Allah without knowledge.﴾ It was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who was very contentious. He used to say: "The angels are the daughters of Allah," and "the Qur'an is the fables of the ancients," and he claimed that Allah is not able to revive one who has decayed and become dust.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿and follows, in that saying and his argument about Allah without knowledge, every devil, rebellious﴾ ﴿It has been decreed for him﴾ it has been decreed upon him, upon the devil ﴿that whoever takes him as an ally, he will mislead him﴾ meaning the devil will mislead, meaning will lead astray whoever takes him as an ally ﴿and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze.﴾ The interpretation of the verse: it has been decreed upon the devil that he will mislead his followers and invite them to the Fire.

Then He established the proof against those who deny resurrection, saying, Mighty is He who speaks: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed We created you﴾ meaning your father Adam, who is the origin of the lineage and the father of humanity, ﴿from dust; then from a sperm-drop﴾ meaning his descendants, ﴿from a sperm-drop﴾, which is semen, and its origin is little water; its plural is nutaf. ﴿Then from a clinging clot﴾, which is congealed fresh blood; its plural is 'alaq. ﴿Then from a lump of flesh, formed and unformed﴾, which is a small piece of flesh about the amount that can be chewed.

Ibn Abbas and Qatada said: complete in creation and incomplete.

Mujahid said: shaped and unshaped, meaning a miscarriage.

'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: When the sperm-drop falls into the womb, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sends an angel who says: "O Lord, formed or unformed?" If He says: "Unformed," the wombs expel it as blood; and if He says: "Formed," the angel says: "O Lord, what is the description of this drop? Male or female? What is its provision? What is its term? Will it be wretched or happy?" Then it is said to him: "Go to the Mother of the Book and copy from it the description of this drop." So the angel goes and copies it, and it remains with him until he reaches the last of its description.

﴿That We may make clear to you﴾ the completeness of Our power and wisdom in Our shaping of the stages of your creation.

﴿And We settle in the wombs﴾ — narrated from 'Asim with a fatha on the ra' in sequence; others read it with a damma, meaning "and We settle," ﴿whom We will﴾, so it is not rejected or aborted, ﴿for an appointed term﴾, until the time of its emergence from the womb with complete form and term. ﴿Then We bring you forth﴾ from your mothers' wombs as ﴿infants﴾, small children; He did not say "children" (atfal), because the Arabs call the plural by the name of the singular.

The poet said:

"Inna al-'awadhil laysa li bi-amir"

and did not say "umara'."

Ibn Jurayj said: [In the second copy: Ibn Jarir] by analogy with the verbal noun, like "'adl" and "zawr." It was also said: by analogy with "khasm" and "daif."

﴿Then that you may reach your full strength﴾, the completeness of your intellects and the limit of your powers.

﴿And among you is one who is taken in death before reaching full strength, and among you is one who is made to live until he is returned to the most abject age﴾, which is senility and dotage, ﴿so that he knows nothing after knowing.﴾

Then He showed another proof of resurrection, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you see the earth lifeless﴾, dry, its traces of crops and plants obliterated, like the extinguishing of fire.

﴿But when We send down upon it water﴾, the rain, ﴿it quivers﴾, moving with vegetation, ﴿and swells﴾, meaning it increases and multiplies the plants with the coming of the rain. Abu Ja'far read "rabat" with a hamza, and similarly in Ha Mim al-Sajda, meaning it rises, grows high and swells, from the Arab saying "raba al-rajul" when a man ascends a high place; and from it the advance guard is called "ri'ba."

﴿And it grows from every lovely pair﴾, a good kind. ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth﴾, and the truth is that which exists and is established, ﴿and that He gives life to the dead, and that He is over all things Powerful, and that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it, and that Allah will resurrect those who are in the graves.﴾

﴿And among mankind is one who argues about Allah without knowledge.﴾ It was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who was very contentious. He used to say: "The angels are the daughters of Allah," and "the Qur'an is the fables of the ancients," and he claimed that Allah is not able to revive one who has decayed and become dust.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿and follows, in that saying and his argument about Allah without knowledge, every devil, rebellious﴾ ﴿It has been decreed for him﴾ it has been decreed upon him, upon the devil ﴿that whoever takes him as an ally, he will mislead him﴾ meaning the devil will mislead, meaning will lead astray whoever takes him as an ally ﴿and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze.﴾ The interpretation of the verse: it has been decreed upon the devil that he will mislead his followers and invite them to the Fire.

Then He established the proof against those who deny resurrection, saying, Mighty is He who speaks: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed We created you﴾ meaning your father Adam, who is the origin of the lineage and the father of humanity, ﴿from dust; then from a sperm-drop﴾ meaning his descendants, ﴿from a sperm-drop﴾, which is semen, and its origin is little water; its plural is nutaf. ﴿Then from a clinging clot﴾, which is congealed fresh blood; its plural is 'alaq. ﴿Then from a lump of flesh, formed and unformed﴾, which is a small piece of flesh about the amount that can be chewed.

Ibn Abbas and Qatada said: complete in creation and incomplete.

Mujahid said: shaped and unshaped, meaning a miscarriage.

'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: When the sperm-drop falls into the womb, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sends an angel who says: "O Lord, formed or unformed?" If He says: "Unformed," the wombs expel it as blood; and if He says: "Formed," the angel says: "O Lord, what is the description of this drop? Male or female? What is its provision? What is its term? Will it be wretched or happy?" Then it is said to him: "Go to the Mother of the Book and copy from it the description of this drop." So the angel goes and copies it, and it remains with him until he reaches the last of its description.

﴿That We may make clear to you﴾ the completeness of Our power and wisdom in Our shaping of the stages of your creation.

﴿And We settle in the wombs﴾ — narrated from 'Asim with a fatha on the ra' in sequence; others read it with a damma, meaning "and We settle," ﴿whom We will﴾, so it is not rejected or aborted, ﴿for an appointed term﴾, until the time of its emergence from the womb with complete form and term. ﴿Then We bring you forth﴾ from your mothers' wombs as ﴿infants﴾, small children; He did not say "children" (atfal), because the Arabs call the plural by the name of the singular.

The poet said:

"Inna al-'awadhil laysa li bi-amir"

and did not say "umara'."

Ibn Jurayj said: [In the second copy: Ibn Jarir] by analogy with the verbal noun, like "'adl" and "zawr." It was also said: by analogy with "khasm" and "daif."

﴿Then that you may reach your full strength﴾, the completeness of your intellects and the limit of your powers.

﴿And among you is one who is taken in death before reaching full strength, and among you is one who is made to live until he is returned to the most abject age﴾, which is senility and dotage, ﴿so that he knows nothing after knowing.﴾

Then He showed another proof of resurrection, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you see the earth lifeless﴾, dry, its traces of crops and plants obliterated, like the extinguishing of fire.

﴿But when We send down upon it water﴾, the rain, ﴿it quivers﴾, moving with vegetation, ﴿and swells﴾, meaning it increases and multiplies the plants with the coming of the rain. Abu Ja'far read "rabat" with a hamza, and similarly in Ha Mim al-Sajda, meaning it rises, grows high and swells, from the Arab saying "raba al-rajul" when a man ascends a high place; and from it the advance guard is called "ri'ba."

﴿And it grows from every lovely pair﴾, a good kind. ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth﴾, and the truth is that which exists and is established, ﴿and that He gives life to the dead, and that He is over all things Powerful, and that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it, and that Allah will resurrect those who are in the graves.﴾

Commentary of al-Tha'labi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 22, verses 1–7:

Makkiyya, except six verses which were revealed in Madina, namely His saying ﴿These are two adversaries who dispute concerning their Lord﴾ up to ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾. It has 5,095 letters, 1,271 words [In the second copy: 1,270 words], and 78 verses.

Abu al-Hasan [In the second copy an addition: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan] al-Jurjani informed us more than once, saying: Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Isma'ili and Abu al-Shaykh Abdullah ibn Muhammad al-Asbahani informed us, both saying: Abu Ishaq Ibrahim ibn Sharik narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn Yunus al-Yarbu'i narrated to us, saying: Sallam ibn Sulaym al-Madaini narrated to us, saying: Harun ibn Kathir narrated to us, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, from Abu Umama, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Surat al-Hajj will be given the reward of a Hajj he performed and an 'Umra he performed, equal to the number of those who performed Hajj and 'Umra in the past and in the future" [1] [[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 7/123.]].

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord. Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing.﴾ Zilzala and zilzal: intense movement in a terrifying state, from the saying "his foot slipped" when it moved quickly from its place, then it was intensified.

﴿The Day you see it﴾

Meaning the Hour.

﴿Every nursing mother will forget﴾

That is, will be preoccupied, according to Ibn Abbas. al-Dahhak said: will be heedless. Ibn Hayyan said: will forget. It is said: "dhahila 'an kadha" meaning he left it and became occupied with something else, "adhhala, yadhulu dhuhulan," and "adhhalani al-shay' idhhalan." The poet said:

"Ṣaḥā qalbuhu yā ʿizz aw kād yadhhal"

﴿every nursing mother﴾

Meaning one who has a nursing child. Murdi'a is the woman who has a child she nurses for another; this is the view of the people of Kufa. The people of Basra said: it is said "imra'a mursi'" when it is intended as a descriptive attribute, like muqrib, mushriq, hamil and ha'id; when they intend the act, they add the ta' marbuta, so one says "murdi'a," the one who nurses her child.

﴿and every pregnant one will drop her load﴾

That is, will cast off her offspring from the terror of that Day.

﴿And you see people as drunkards, but they are not drunkards.﴾

al-Hasan [In the second copy: al-Husayn] said: its meaning: "and you see people as drunkards" from fear, "but they are not drunkards" from wine.

The people of meaning (ahl al-ma'ani) said: its figurative sense is "and you see people as if they were drunkards," supported by the reading of Abu Zur'a ibn 'Amr ibn Jarir: "wa-turā al-nās" with a dammed ta', meaning "they are thought to be."

The people of Kufa, except 'Asim, read "sukra" and "ma hum bi-sukra" without alif in both, and both are two dialects for the plural of drunkard, like kusala and kasala.

﴿But the punishment of Allah is severe.﴾

ʿImran ibn Husayn, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and others narrated that these two verses were revealed at night during the expedition of Bani al-Mustaliq, who were a tribe of Khuza'a, while the people were traveling. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called out, so they urged their mounts until they were around the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he recited them to them. No one wept more than on that night. When they woke in the morning, they did not unsaddle the beasts, did not pitch the tents, and did not cook any pot, while people were among weeping, bare-headed, sorrowful and pensive. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them [In the second copy an addition: "Do you know which day that is?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "That is the day when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will say to Adam: 'Arise and send forth the company of the Fire from your offspring.' Adam will say: 'From every how many?' Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will say: 'From every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine to the Fire and one to Paradise.' This was heavy upon the Muslims, and they wept and said: 'Then who will be saved, O Messenger of Allah?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said.]: "Rejoice, be steadfast and be near to the mark, for with you are two creatures which have never been in any people without multiplying them: Gog and Magog."

Then he said: "Indeed I hope you will be a quarter of the people of Paradise," so they proclaimed takbir and praised Allah. Then he said: "Indeed I hope you will be a third of the people of Paradise," so they proclaimed takbir and praised Allah. Then he said: "Indeed I hope you will be half of the people of Paradise," so they proclaimed takbir and praised Allah. Then he said: "Indeed I hope you will be two-thirds of the people of Paradise. The people of Paradise are one hundred and twenty rows, eighty of them are my community, and the Muslims among the disbelievers are not but like a mole on the flank of a camel or a spot on the foreleg of a beast, rather like a black hair on a white bull or a white hair on a black bull." Then he said: "And seventy thousand of my community will enter Paradise without reckoning." 'Umar said: "Seventy thousand?" He said: "Yes, and with each one seventy thousand." Then 'Ukasha ibn Mihsan stood up and said: "O Messenger of Allah, pray to Allah that He make me one of them." He said: "You are one of them." Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 22, verse 8–18:

﴿And among the people is he who disputes concerning God without knowledge or guidance or an illuminating Book﴾. It was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. ﴿Turning aside (thani 'atfihi)﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal).

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Arrogant within himself. The Arabs say: 'So-and-so came thani 'atfihi,' meaning haughty, due to his pride and arrogance. The 'atf (flank) is the side."

al-Dahhak: "Lifting up his nose disdainfully." Mujahid and Qatadah: "Twisting his neck (lawiyan 'unuqahu)." ['Ata' and Ibn Zayd: "Turning away from what he is called to out of pride."]

Ibn Jurayj: "That is, he turns away from the truth. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿When Our verses are recited to him, he turns away in arrogance﴾ [Luqman 31:7], and His saying: ﴿When it is said to them, 'Come, the Messenger of God will ask forgiveness for you,' they turn their heads aside﴾ [al-Munafiqun 63:5]."

﴿To mislead from the way of God. For him in this world is disgrace﴾: punishment, humiliation and degradation, which was his being killed at Badr.

﴿And We will make him taste on the Day of Resurrection the punishment of the Burning﴾. It will be said to him on that day: ﴿This is for what your hands have sent forth﴾ — and this and its like is an intensification in attributing the sin to him.

﴿And indeed God is not unjust to the servants﴾, so as to punish them without sin. He, glory be to Him, in whatever manner He disposes of His servant, is not unjust; rather, the unjust is the transgressor who domineers over what is not his own.

﴿And among the people is he who worships God on an edge (harf)﴾, the verse.

It was revealed concerning Bedouins who used to come to the Messenger of God ﷺ in Medina as emigrants from their desert. When one of them came to Medina: if his body was healthy there, and his mare foaled a fine foal, and his wife bore a boy, and his wealth and livestock increased, he was content with it and reassured by it, and said: "I have not encountered anything since I entered this religion of mine but good." But if the sickness of Medina afflicted him, and his wife bore a girl, and his mares miscarried, and his wealth went away, and the charity was delayed from him, the Devil came to him and said: "By God, you have encountered nothing since you were upon this religion of yours but evil," and he would turn back from his religion. That is the trial. So God, glory be to Him, revealed: ﴿And among the people is he who worships God on an edge﴾.

That is, on one side and one border of the religion, not entering it with steadfastness and firm establishment. Harf means the extremity of a body. Mujahid said: "On doubt."

Some of the people of meanings said: he means "with weakness in worship, like one standing on an edge, unsteady in it."

Some of them said: he means "in one uniform state in all circumstances, following his own desire. Had they worshipped God in thanks in prosperity and patience in adversity, they would not have worshipped God on an edge." [In the second manuscript: "on its fear."]

al-Hasan said: he is the hypocrite who worships with his tongue without his heart.

﴿If good befalls him﴾: health in his body and ease in his livelihood, ﴿he is reassured by it﴾, meaning he is content with it, reassured by it, and remains upon it.

﴿But if a trial befalls him﴾: affliction in his body, constraint in his livelihood, and the frustration of what he desires in his condition, ﴿he turns back upon his face﴾: he apostatizes and returns to the face he had before, which is disbelief. ﴿He has lost this world and the Hereafter.﴾ Hamid al-A'raj and Ya'qub read khasira al-dunya ("the one who has lost the world") with an alif, in the pattern of fa'il, and "and the Hereafter" in the genitive, as a circumstantial qualifier.

﴿That is the manifest loss.﴾ ﴿He calls upon, besides God, that which neither harms him if he disobeys, nor benefits him if he obeys, after having embraced Islam and returning to his disbelief. That is the far-off error﴾, he has gone far astray from the truth.

﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾. The grammarians differed concerning the function of this lam. Some said it is a complement (silah), its sense being: "he calls upon him whose harm is nearer than his benefit." Thus Ibn Mas'ud read it. al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj claimed that the lam means postponement, its estimate being: "He calls upon—by God—one whose harm is nearer than his benefit."

Some said: this is for emphasis, meaning: "He calls upon, for one whose harm is nearer than his benefit, he calls upon," then the last "calls upon" was deleted, relying on the first. If you say: "You strike for one whose good is greater than his evil, you strike," and then delete the last, it is permissible.

It is related from the Arabs by hearing: "I gave you for what is other than it is better than it," and "at him for what is other than it is better than it."

It was also said: "He calls upon (yad'u) for one whose harm..." is from His saying: "That is the far-off error," and the place of "that" is accusative by "calls upon," as if He said: "That which is the far-off error, he calls upon," then He resumed and said: "for one whose harm is nearer than his benefit," and "man" is in the nominative position by inception, its predicate being: ﴿Evil is the patron and evil is the companion﴾.

It was also said: "yad'u" here means "says," and the predicate is omitted, its estimate being: "for one whose harm is nearer than his benefit—his god—is evil the patron (al-mawla), the helper, and evil the companion (al-'ashir), the associate, the comrade and intimate," meaning the idol.

﴿Indeed God will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. Indeed God does what He wills.﴾

﴿Whoever thinks that God will not help him in this world and the Hereafter﴾: the commentators differed regarding the referent of the pronoun in "yansurahu" (He will help him). Most exegetes said it refers to His Prophet ﷺ. Qatadah said: it means, "whoever thinks that God will not help His Prophet, then let him stretch a rope to the sky," to the ceiling of the house, "and let him hang himself with it until he dies; then let him cut the rope after strangulation, and then let him see whether his scheming, his device, removes what enrages him." This is the statement of most interpreters, but the meaning of the verse is: let him picture this matter in his own mind; he is not to actually do it, because if he strangles himself and dies, he cannot cut and look.

al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: this is like saying in speech to an envious or obstinate person: "If you are not pleased with this, then hang yourself."

Ibn Zayd said: "The sky in this verse is the sky known by its very name," and he said: the meaning of the speech is: whoever thinks that God will not help His Prophet and will contend with him in his religion and affair, seeking to sever it from him, let him cut that off at its root, from where it comes to him, for its root is in heaven. ﴿Let him stretch a rope to the sky, then let him cut off from the Prophet ﷺ the revelation that comes to him from God,﴾ for he will not contend with him until his root is severed from him. "Then let him see whether he is able to remove his rage by this act."

It is mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning a group from Asad and Ghatafan who were slow to embrace Islam and said: "We fear that Muhammad will not be helped, and so the bond between us and our allies among the Jews will be severed, and they will not supply us with provisions nor give us shelter." So God said to them: whoever seeks to hasten from God the victory of Muhammad, let him hang himself, and let him see whether his hastening in this matter removes his rage within himself. Likewise, his hastening from God the victory of Muhammad will not bring forward His help before its appointed time.

Mujahid said: the pronoun in "yansurahu" refers to "man," and the meaning of the speech is: whoever thinks that God will not provide for him in this world and the Hereafter, let him stretch a rope to the sky of the house and hang himself; let him see whether his act removes what enrages him, which is his strangulation by not being provided for. On this view, "nasr" (help) means provision, as the Arabs say: "Whoever helps me, God helps him," meaning whoever gives me, God gives him.

Abu 'Ubayd said: the Arabs say "ard mansurah," meaning "rained upon," as if God had given it rain.

al-Fiq'asi [in the second manuscript: "the poet said"] said:

"And you will not give a man beyond his right, nor will you possess the stretch of land which the rain has helped."

[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 12/22.]

Regarding His saying "ma yaghiz" (what enrages), the Arabic grammarians have two opinions: one, that it means "alladhi" (which), its estimate being: "let him see whether his scheming removes that which enrages him," and the pronoun is deleted for lightness. The second, that it is a verbal noun, its estimate being: "let him see whether his scheming removes his rage."

﴿Thus We have sent it down as clear signs, and indeed God guides whom He wills.﴾ ﴿Indeed those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabeans, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associate partners (with God)﴾, meaning the worshippers of idols. Qatadah said: "The religions are five: four belong to Satan and one to the Merciful." ﴿Indeed God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed God is over all things a witness.﴾ The grammarians said: "Inna Allah" is the predicate of "inna alladhina," as you say: "Inna Zaydan inna al-khayra 'indahu lakathir," like the verse of the poet:

"Indeed the caliph—indeed God has clothed him in a garment of kingship, by which the seals are hoped for."

[Lisan al-'Arab: 12/164.]

﴿Have you not seen, with your heart and intellect, that to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon and the stars, and the mountains and the trees and the creatures﴾.

Mujahid said: their prostration is the shifting of their shadows. Abu al-'Aliyah said: there is no star, nor sun, nor moon in the sky but it falls prostrate to God when it sets, and then it does not turn until it is given permission, and it takes the right-hand course when it returns to its rising place.

The people of realities said: the prostration of inanimate things and what has no intellect is the humble submission and subjugation within them, and the traces of craftsmanship and formation which call the rational to prostrate to God, glory be to Him, as the poet said:

"And in everything there is a sign of His, indicating that He is One."

[Taj al-'Arus: 9/398.]

﴿And many among the people, and many have deserved the punishment﴾: for their disbelief, while, despite that, their shadows prostrate to God. Mujahid said... Some said: it means prostrating to God, that is, submitting to Him and acknowledging what their intellect requires and compels them to, even if they disbelieve in other matters.

They said: in His saying "and many have deserved the punishment" there is the conjunctive waw. Some said it is the waw of resumption, meaning: "and many have deserved the punishment" for their disbelief and refusal to prostrate.

Abu al-Qasim ibn Habib related to me from Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash that he said: there is an ellipsis in the verse, its estimate being: "And many of the people prostrated, and many refused, and have deserved the punishment."

﴿And whoever God humiliates, there is for him no honorer.﴾ That is, whom God humiliates. The common readers read "mukrim" with a kasra on the ra'. Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Aylah [in the second manuscript: Ibn 'Aylah] read "mukram" with a fatha on the ra', meaning honor (ikram), as in His saying: ﴿Cause me to enter a sound entrance﴾ [al-Isra' 17:80] and ﴿cause me to land a blessed landing﴾ [Musnad Ahmad 2:314], meaning entrance and landing.

﴿Indeed God does what He wills.﴾

When one of them came to Medina: if his body was healthy there, and his mare foaled a fine foal, and his wife bore a boy, and his wealth and livestock increased, he was content with it and reassured by it, and said: "I have not encountered anything since I entered this religion of mine but good." But if the sickness of Medina afflicted him, and his wife bore a girl, and his mares miscarried, and his wealth went away, and the charity was delayed from him, the Devil came to him and said: "By God, you have encountered nothing since you were upon this religion of yours but evil," and he would turn back from his religion. That is the trial. So God, glory be to Him, revealed: ﴿And among the people is he who worships God on an edge﴾.

That is, on one side and one border of the religion, not entering it with steadfastness and firm establishment. Harf means the extremity of a body. Mujahid said: "On doubt."

Some of the people of meanings said: he means "with weakness in worship, like one standing on an edge, unsteady in it."

Some of them said: he means "in one uniform state in all circumstances, following his own desire. Had they worshipped God in thanks in prosperity and patience in adversity, they would not have worshipped God on an edge." [In the second manuscript: "on its fear."]

al-Hasan said: he is the hypocrite who worships with his tongue without his heart.

﴿If good befalls him﴾: health in his body and ease in his livelihood, ﴿he is reassured by it﴾, meaning he is content with it, reassured by it, and remains upon it.

﴿But if a trial befalls him﴾: affliction in his body, constraint in his livelihood, and the frustration of what he desires in his condition, ﴿he turns back upon his face﴾: he apostatizes and returns to the face he had before, which is disbelief. ﴿He has lost this world and the Hereafter.﴾ Hamid al-A'raj and Ya'qub read khasira al-dunya ("the one who has lost the world") with an alif, in the pattern of fa'il, and "and the Hereafter" in the genitive, as a circumstantial qualifier.

﴿That is the manifest loss.﴾ ﴿He calls upon, besides God, that which neither harms him if he disobeys, nor benefits him if he obeys, after having embraced Islam and returning to his disbelief. That is the far-off error﴾, he has gone far astray from the truth.

﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾. The grammarians differed concerning the function of this lam. Some said it is a complement (silah), its sense being: "he calls upon him whose harm is nearer than his benefit." Thus Ibn Mas'ud read it. al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj claimed that the lam means postponement, its estimate being: "He calls upon—by God—one whose harm is nearer than his benefit."

Some said: this is for emphasis, meaning: "He calls upon, for one whose harm is nearer than his benefit, he calls upon," then the last "calls upon" was deleted, relying on the first. If you say: "You strike for one whose good is greater than his evil, you strike," and then delete the last, it is permissible.

It is related from the Arabs by hearing: "I gave you for what is other than it is better than it," and "at him for what is other than it is better than it."

It was also said: "He calls upon (yad'u) for one whose harm..." is from His saying: "That is the far-off error," and the place of "that" is accusative by "calls upon," as if He said: "That which is the far-off error, he calls upon," then He resumed and said: "for one whose harm is nearer than his benefit," and "man" is in the nominative position by inception, its predicate being: ﴿Evil is the patron and evil is the companion﴾.

It was also said: "yad'u" here means "says," and the predicate is omitted, its estimate being: "for one whose harm is nearer than his benefit—his god—is evil the patron (al-mawla), the helper, and evil the companion (al-'ashir), the associate, the comrade and intimate," meaning the idol.

﴿Indeed God will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. Indeed God does what He wills.﴾

﴿Whoever thinks that God will not help him in this world and the Hereafter﴾: the commentators differed regarding the referent of the pronoun in "yansurahu" (He will help him). Most exegetes said it refers to His Prophet ﷺ. Qatadah said: it means, "whoever thinks that God will not help His Prophet, then let him stretch a rope to the sky," to the ceiling of the house, "and let him hang himself with it until he dies; then let him cut the rope after strangulation, and then let him see whether his scheming, his device, removes what enrages him." This is the statement of most interpreters, but the meaning of the verse is: let him picture this matter in his own mind; he is not to actually do it, because if he strangles himself and dies, he cannot cut and look.

al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: this is like saying in speech to an envious or obstinate person: "If you are not pleased with this, then hang yourself."

Ibn Zayd said: "The sky in this verse is the sky known by its very name," and he said: the meaning of the speech is: whoever thinks that God will not help His Prophet and will contend with him in his religion and affair, seeking to sever it from him, let him cut that off at its root, from where it comes to him, for its root is in heaven. ﴿Let him stretch a rope to the sky, then let him cut off from the Prophet ﷺ the revelation that comes to him from God,﴾ for he will not contend with him until his root is severed from him. "Then let him see whether he is able to remove his rage by this act."

It is mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning a group from Asad and Ghatafan who were slow to embrace Islam and said: "We fear that Muhammad will not be helped, and so the bond between us and our allies among the Jews will be severed, and they will not supply us with provisions nor give us shelter." So God said to them: whoever seeks to hasten from God the victory of Muhammad, let him hang himself, and let him see whether his hastening in this matter removes his rage within himself. Likewise, his hastening from God the victory of Muhammad will not bring forward His help before its appointed time.

Mujahid said: the pronoun in "yansurahu" refers to "man," and the meaning of the speech is: whoever thinks that God will not provide for him in this world and the Hereafter, let him stretch a rope to the sky of the house and hang himself; let him see whether his act removes what enrages him, which is his strangulation by not being provided for. On this view, "nasr" (help) means provision, as the Arabs say: "Whoever helps me, God helps him," meaning whoever gives me, God gives him.

Abu 'Ubayd said: the Arabs say "ard mansurah," meaning "rained upon," as if God had given it rain.

al-Fiq'asi [in the second manuscript: "the poet said"] said:

"And you will not give a man beyond his right, nor will you possess the stretch of land which the rain has helped."

[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 12/22.]

Regarding His saying "ma yaghiz" (what enrages), the Arabic grammarians have two opinions: one, that it means "alladhi" (which), its estimate being: "let him see whether his scheming removes that which enrages him," and the pronoun is deleted for lightness. The second, that it is a verbal noun, its estimate being: "let him see whether his scheming removes his rage."

[Lisan al-'Arab: 12/164.]

﴿Have you not seen, with your heart and intellect, that to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon and the stars, and the mountains and the trees and the creatures﴾.

Abu al-'Aliyah said: there is no star, nor sun, nor moon in the sky but it falls prostrate to God when it sets, and then it does not turn until it is given permission, and it takes the right-hand course when it returns to its rising place.

The people of realities said: the prostration of inanimate things and what has no intellect is the humble submission and subjugation within them, and the traces of craftsmanship and formation which call the rational to prostrate to God, glory be to Him, as the poet said:

"And in everything there is a sign of His, indicating that He is One."

[Taj al-'Arus: 9/398.]

Some said: it means prostrating to God, that is, submitting to Him and acknowledging what their intellect requires and compels them to, even if they disbelieve in other matters.

They said: in His saying "and many have deserved the punishment" there is the conjunctive waw. Some said it is the waw of resumption, meaning: "and many have deserved the punishment" for their disbelief and refusal to prostrate.

﴿And indeed God is not unjust to the servants﴾, so as to punish them without sin. He, glory be to Him, in whatever manner He disposes of His servant, is not unjust; rather, the unjust is the transgressor who domineers over what is not his own.

﴿And among the people is he who worships God on an edge (harf)﴾, the verse.

But if the sickness of Medina afflicted him, and his wife bore a girl, and his mares miscarried, and his wealth went away, and the charity was delayed from him, the Devil came to him and said: "By God, you have encountered nothing since you were upon this religion of yours but evil," and he would turn back from his religion. That is the trial. So God, glory be to Him, revealed: ﴿And among the people is he who worships God on an edge﴾.

That is, on one side and one border of the religion, not entering it with steadfastness and firm establishment. Harf means the extremity of a body. Mujahid said: "On doubt."

Some of the people of meanings said: he means "with weakness in worship, like one standing on an edge, unsteady in it."

Some of them said: he means "in one uniform state in all circumstances, following his own desire. Had they worshipped God in thanks in prosperity and patience in adversity, they would not have worshipped God on an edge." [In the second manuscript: "on its fear."]

al-Hasan said: he is the hypocrite who worships with his tongue without his heart.

﴿If good befalls him﴾: health in his body and ease in his livelihood, ﴿he is reassured by it﴾, meaning he is content with it, reassured by it, and remains upon it.

﴿But if a trial befalls him﴾: affliction in his body, constraint in his livelihood, and the frustration of what he desires in his condition, ﴿he turns back upon his face﴾: he apostatizes and returns to the face he had before, which is disbelief. ﴿He has lost this world and the Hereafter.﴾ Hamid al-A'raj and Ya'qub read khasira al-dunya ("the one who has lost the world") with an alif, in the pattern of fa'il, and "and the Hereafter" in the genitive, as a circumstantial qualifier.

﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾. The grammarians differed concerning the function of this lam. Some said it is a complement (silah), its sense being: "he calls upon him whose harm is nearer than his benefit." Thus Ibn Mas'ud read it. al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj claimed that the lam means postponement, its estimate being: "He calls upon—by God—one whose harm is nearer than his benefit."

Some said: this is for emphasis, meaning: "He calls upon, for one whose harm is nearer than his benefit, he calls upon," then the last "calls upon" was deleted, relying on the first. If you say: "You strike for one whose good is greater than his evil, you strike," and then delete the last, it is permissible.

It is related from the Arabs by hearing: "I gave you for what is other than it is better than it," and "at him for what is other than it is better than it."

It was also said: "He calls upon (yad'u) for one whose harm..." is from His saying: "That is the far-off error," and the place of "that" is accusative by "calls upon," as if He said: "That which is the far-off error, he calls upon," then He resumed and said: "for one whose harm is nearer than his benefit," and "man" is in the nominative position by inception, its predicate being: ﴿Evil is the patron and evil is the companion﴾.

It was also said: "yad'u" here means "says," and the predicate is omitted, its estimate being: "for one whose harm is nearer than his benefit—his god—is evil the patron (al-mawla), the helper, and evil the companion (al-'ashir), the associate, the comrade and intimate," meaning the idol.

﴿Indeed God will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. Indeed God does what He wills.﴾

﴿Whoever thinks that God will not help him in this world and the Hereafter﴾: the commentators differed regarding the referent of the pronoun in "yansurahu" (He will help him). Most exegetes said it refers to His Prophet ﷺ. Qatadah said: it means, "whoever thinks that God will not help His Prophet, then let him stretch a rope to the sky," to the ceiling of the house, "and let him hang himself with it until he dies; then let him cut the rope after strangulation, and then let him see whether his scheming, his device, removes what enrages him." This is the statement of most interpreters, but the meaning of the verse is: let him picture this matter in his own mind; he is not to actually do it, because if he strangles himself and dies, he cannot cut and look.

al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: this is like saying in speech to an envious or obstinate person: "If you are not pleased with this, then hang yourself."

Ibn Zayd said: "The sky in this verse is the sky known by its very name," and he said: the meaning of the speech is: whoever thinks that God will not help His Prophet and will contend with him in his religion and affair, seeking to sever it from him, let him cut that off at its root, from where it comes to him, for its root is in heaven. ﴿Let him stretch a rope to the sky, then let him cut off from the Prophet ﷺ the revelation that comes to him from God,﴾ for he will not contend with him until his root is severed from him. It is mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning a group from Asad and Ghatafan who were slow to embrace Islam and said: "We fear that Muhammad will not be helped, and so the bond between us and our allies among the Jews will be severed, and they will not supply us with provisions nor give us shelter." Abu 'Ubayd said: the Arabs say "ard mansurah," meaning "rained upon," as if God had given it rain.

al-Fiq'asi [in the second manuscript: "the poet said"] said:

"And you will not give a man beyond his right, nor will you possess the stretch of land which the rain has helped."

[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 12/22.]

The second, that it is a verbal noun, its estimate being: "let him see whether his scheming removes his rage."

Qatadah said: "The religions are five: four belong to Satan and one to the Merciful." ﴿Indeed God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. "Indeed the caliph—indeed God has clothed him in a garment of kingship, by which the seals are hoped for."

[Lisan al-'Arab: 12/164.]

"And in everything there is a sign of His, indicating that He is One."

[Taj al-'Arus: 9/398.]

They said: in His saying "and many have deserved the punishment" there is the conjunctive waw. Some said it is the waw of resumption, meaning: "and many have deserved the punishment" for their disbelief and refusal to prostrate.

Abu al-Qasim ibn Habib related to me from Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash that he said: there is an ellipsis in the verse, its estimate being: "And many of the people prostrated, and many refused, and have deserved the punishment."

Indeed God is over all things a witness.﴾ The grammarians said: "Inna Allah" is the predicate of "inna alladhina," as you say: "Inna Zaydan inna al-khayra 'indahu lakathir," like the verse of the poet:

"Indeed the caliph—indeed God has clothed him in a garment of kingship, by which the seals are hoped for."

[Lisan al-'Arab: 12/164.]

﴿Have you not seen, with your heart and intellect, that to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon and the stars, and the mountains and the trees and the creatures﴾.

Mujahid said: their prostration is the shifting of their shadows. Abu al-'Aliyah said: there is no star, nor sun, nor moon in the sky but it falls prostrate to God when it sets, and then it does not turn until it is given permission, and it takes the right-hand course when it returns to its rising place.

The people of realities said: the prostration of inanimate things and what has no intellect is the humble submission and subjugation within them, and the traces of craftsmanship and formation which call the rational to prostrate to God, glory be to Him, as the poet said:

"And in everything there is a sign of His, indicating that He is One."

[Taj al-'Arus: 9/398.]

﴿And many among the people, and many have deserved the punishment﴾: for their disbelief, while, despite that, their shadows prostrate to God. Mujahid said... Some said: it means prostrating to God, that is, submitting to Him and acknowledging what their intellect requires and compels them to, even if they disbelieve in other matters.

They said: in His saying "and many have deserved the punishment" there is the conjunctive waw. Some said it is the waw of resumption, meaning: "and many have deserved the punishment" for their disbelief and refusal to prostrate.

Abu al-Qasim ibn Habib related to me from Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash that he said: there is an ellipsis in the verse, its estimate being: "And many of the people prostrated, and many refused, and have deserved the punishment."

﴿And whoever God humiliates, there is for him no honorer.﴾ That is, whom God humiliates. The common readers read "mukrim" with a kasra on the ra'. Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Aylah [in the second manuscript: Ibn 'Aylah] read "mukram" with a fatha on the ra', meaning honor (ikram), as in His saying: ﴿Cause me to enter a sound entrance﴾ [al-Isra' 17:80] and ﴿cause me to land a blessed landing﴾ [Musnad Ahmad 2:314], meaning entrance and landing.

﴿Indeed God does what He wills.﴾

This is the commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 22, verses 19–26:

These two adversaries (khasmani) who dispute concerning their Lord: that is, concerning His religion and His command. The word khasm (adversary) is a noun resembling a verbal noun (wasf al-masdar), and for this reason He said ikhtasamu ("they disputed"), like His words: ﴿And has the story of the adversaries reached you, when they climbed over the wall into the prayer-chamber?﴾ [Sad 21].

The exegetes differed concerning these two adversaries: who are they?

Qays ibn 'Abbad narrated that Abu Dharr al-Ghifari used to swear by Allah, the Exalted, that this verse was revealed concerning six men of Quraysh who challenged one another on the day of Badr: Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, 'Utbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabi'ah, al-Walid ibn 'Utbah, and 'Ubaydah ibn al-Harith. He said:

And 'Ali said: "I will indeed be the first to kneel in dispute before Allah, the Exalted, on the Day of Resurrection."

To this view went Hilal ibn Nassaf and 'Ata' ibn Yasar. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the People of the Book, who said to the believers: "We have a greater claim to Allah and are earlier in scripture than you, and our Prophet came before your Prophet." The believers said: "We have a greater claim to Allah. We believed in Muhammad (ﷺ) and we believed in your Prophet and in what Allah, the Exalted, sent down of scripture. You know our scripture and our Prophet, then you abandoned it and disbelieved in it out of envy." This was their dispute concerning their Lord.

Mujahid, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, 'Asim ibn Abi al-Najud and al-Kalbi said: they are the believers and the disbelievers, all of them, of whatever religion they were.

'Ikrimah said: they are Paradise and Hell, which disputed: Hell said, "Allah created me for His punishment," and Paradise said, "Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, created me for His mercy." Allah, the Exalted, has related to you of their story what you hear. The evidence for this interpretation is what

Abu Sa'id ibn Hamdun, may Allah have mercy on him, reported to us by my reading to him, saying: Abu Hamid ibn al-Sharqi reported to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Dhuhli, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Bishr al-'Abdi and Ahmad ibn Yusuf al-Sulami told us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq ibn Hammam al-Himyari told us, saying: Ma'mar ibn Rashid reported to us from Hammam ibn Munabbih, who said: This is what Abu Hurayrah related to us from Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Paradise and Hell disputed. Hell said: 'I have been given the arrogant and the tyrannical.' Paradise said: 'Only the weak among people and their rejects will enter me.' Allah said to Paradise: 'You are My mercy; I show mercy through you to whomever I will of My servants.' And He said to Hell: 'You are My punishment; I punish through you whomever I will of My servants. Each of you will be filled.' As for Hell, they will be cast into it and it will say: ﴿Is there more?﴾ It will not be filled until Allah places His foot upon it, whereupon it says: 'Enough, enough, enough,' and then it is filled, and parts of it draw in upon one another, and Allah does not wrong any of His creation. As for Paradise, Allah will create for it a new creation."

Then He explained the end of the two adversaries and the condition of the people of the two abodes, saying, the Exalted: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "garments of fire" means garments of copper made of fire, and there is nothing among vessels that, when heated, is more intense in heat than it.

﴿Boiling water will be poured over their heads﴾: hot water.

Abu Hurayrah reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed the boiling water will be poured upon their heads, and it will penetrate the skull until it reaches the inside of the body and dissolves what is in its belly until it reaches their feet, and this is al-sahr (melting). Then they will be restored as they were."

﴿By which what is in their bellies will be melted﴾: it is melted. It is said: "sahharat al-alyah wa al-shahm bi al-nar" — I melted the fat-tail and the tallow with fire; I melt it, melting it. The poet said:

You see the ... cast in a barren plain, the sun melts it and it does not melt.

The meaning of the verse: by the boiling water poured over their heads, what is in their bellies of fats and entrails is melted, and their skins are scorched and fall off.

﴿And for them are hooks of iron (maqami' sawt min hadid)﴾: its singular is miqma'ah; it was named so because the one struck is subdued (yuqma'u) by it, that is, humbled.

﴿Whenever they wish to get out of it, from distress, they will be returned into it﴾: they are sent back into it.

Al-A'mash related from Abu Zabyan, who said: it was mentioned that they try to leave the Fire when Hell surges, and it throws them up to its upper gates, and they wish to get out of it, but the guards of it punish them and return them to it with the hooks, and they say to them: ﴿And taste the punishment of the burning﴾, that is, the burning one, like "painful" and "agonizing." And "taste" (dhawq) is the sense by which the perception of flavor is obtained; here it is used figuratively, and what is meant is their perception of pains.

﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believed and did righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow; they will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾, where it is the plural of siwar; and pearls (wa lu'lu'an).

ʿĀṣim and the people of Madinah here and in Surah al-Mala'ikah read wa lu'lu'an with the accusative, in the sense of "and they will be adorned with pearls," and they cited that it is written with an alif in all the codices here.

The rest read it in the genitive, as a conjunction with gold. Then they differed concerning the reason for the alif written in it: Abu 'Amr said the alif was written in it just as it was written in qalu and kanu; al-Kisa'i said they wrote it for the hamzah, because the hamzah is one of the letters. As for Ya'qub, he read it here in the accusative and in Surah Fatir in the genitive, returning to the codex, since it is written in all the codices here with an alif and there without an alif.

﴿And their clothing therein is silk﴾, and ﴿they were guided to good speech﴾, which is the testimony that there is no god but Allah. Ibn Zayd said: "There is no god but Allah, Allah is greatest, and praise belongs to Allah." Its parallel is His words: ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾ [Fatir 10], and ﴿they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy﴾, to the religion of Allah.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar (wa yasudduna)﴾: he used the present after the past, because the barring is in the sense of the continuity of the attribute for them. The meaning of the verse: they are barring, and it is their habit to bar. Its parallel is His words: ﴿those who believed and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Ra'd 28]. It was also said: the wording is present but the meaning is past, i.e., and they barred from the way of Allah and from the Masjid, meaning from al-Masjid al-Haram, ﴿which We have made (ja'alnahu)﴾, created and built, ﴿for the people﴾, all of them; We did not single out some of them over others, ﴿equal (sawa'an)﴾: ﴿the one who dwells there (al-'Akif)﴾, the resident, ﴿and the visitor (al-Bad)﴾, the one who comes to it from elsewhere.

ʿĀṣim, according to the narration of Hafs, and Ya'qub, according to the narration of Rawh, read sawa'an in the accusative, with the act of making falling upon it, since the verb "make" takes two objects.

The others read it in the nominative, as the subject, with what follows it as the predicate. The complete statement ends at His words ﴿for the people﴾.

The scholars differed concerning the meaning of the verse. Some said: "equal are the one who dwells there and the visitor" in honoring its sanctity, performing rites there, and the right of Allah that is obligatory upon both of them in it; this is the view of Mujahid.

Others said: they are equal in alighting there, so neither of them has a greater claim than the other to any place in it. By this verse they forbade the renting of the houses of Makkah, and disliked letting them out during the season.

'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar said: "Equal, whether you eat forbidden food or rent a house in Makkah."

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit said: when the pilgrims came to Makkah, none of the people of Makkah had a greater right to his dwelling than they did; so a man who found room would alight. Then theft spread among them, and each person stole from his own side. A man made a door, and 'Umar sent to him: "Have you made a door against the pilgrims of the House of Allah?" He said: "No, I only made it to guard their goods." And this is His words: ﴿equal, the one who dwells there and the visitor﴾.

He said: the visitor there is like the resident; no one has a greater right to a dwelling than another, unless one has preceded to a dwelling. To this view went Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Zayd and Badhan, who said: they are equal in houses and dwellings. The first view is nearer to the truth.

Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan reported to us by my reading to him, saying: Safwan ibn al-Husayn told us, saying:

Abu Muhammad ibn Abi Hatim told us, saying: I heard Abu Isma'il al-Tirmidhi in Makkah in the year 260 say: I heard Ishaq ibn Rahawayh say: I sat with al-Shafi'i in Makkah, and we discussed the renting of houses in Makkah. He permitted it, and I did not permit it. Al-Shafi'i mentioned a hadith and fell silent, and I began on the chapter, reciting it at length; when I finished, I said to a companion of mine from the people of Marw in Persian: "Mard kama li ani hast qariyah bi Marw" (a man, what do I have, is there a village in Marw), and he understood that I had spoken to my companion in a language that disparaged him. He said to me: "Will you debate?" I said: "I came for debate." He said: Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿those who were expelled from their homes﴾ [Al 'Imran 195] — did He attribute the homes to their owners or not to their owners? And the Prophet (ﷺ) said on the day of the Conquest of Makkah: "Whoever closes his door is safe, and whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe. Has 'Aqil left us any houses?" He attributed the house to its owners or not to its owners? And he said to me: "Did 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, buy the prison house from its owner or not from its owner?" When I knew that the proof had been established against me, I stood up.

﴿And whoever intends therein (fihi), in the Sacred Mosque, with deviation, in wrongdoing﴾: that is, deviation by wrongdoing, which is inclining toward injustice; and the ba' in it is extra, like His words: ﴿grows with the oil (tanbutu bi al-duhn)﴾, that is, grows the oil.

Al-Farra' said: I heard a Bedouin from Rabi'ah, and I asked him about something, and he said: "arju bi dhalika," meaning "arju dhalika" (I hope for that).

And a poet said:

In a valley of Yemen, the shit grows at its breast, and at its base with al-markh and al-shabahan.

That is, al-markh. Al-A'sha said:

We guaranteed the provision of our dependents by our spears, between the cauldrons and the bare-ridged sword.

Meaning: our spears guaranteed the provision of our dependents. Another said:

Has it not reached you, while the news spreads, what the she-camels of the Banu Ziyad suffered?

They differed concerning the meaning of the verse. Mujahid and Qatadah said: ﴿whoever intends therein with deviation, in wrongdoing﴾ is shirk, that one worships other than Allah, the Exalted, therein.

Others said: it is making lawful what is forbidden and committing sins therein.

Ibn Mas'ud said: No man intends an evil deed and it is written against him; even if a man in Aden or another land intends to kill a man in Makkah, or intends an evil deed there without doing it, Allah will make him taste the painful punishment.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it is that you kill there one who does not kill you, or wrong one who does not wrong you. This view is the meaning of the saying of al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd.

Ahmad ibn Abi ... reported to us, saying: al-Mughirah ibn 'Amr reported to us, saying: al-Mufaddal ibn Muhammad told us, saying: Muhammad ibn Yusuf told us, saying: Abu Qurrah told us, saying: Sufyan mentioned from Layth, from Mujahid, that he said: Evil deeds are multiplied in Makkah just as good deeds are multiplied.

Ibn Jurayj: it is making lawful the forbidden deliberately. From Habib ibn Abi Thabit: hoarding food in Makkah. Some said: it is everything that was forbidden of speech and action, even the speaker's saying: "No, by Allah," and "Yes, by Allah."

Shu'bah narrated from Mansur, from Mujahid, from Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, that he had two tents, one in the area outside the sanctuary and the other within the sanctuary; if he wished to rebuke his family, he rebuked them in the other one. When he was asked about that, he said: "We used to hear that among deviation therein is that a man says: 'No, by Allah,' and 'Yes, by Allah.'"

﴿And when We settled (wa idh bawwa'na)﴾: we placed it (wa ṭṭa'na). Ibn 'Abbas said: we made it; al-Hasan: we brought down; Muqatil ibn Sulayman: we guided him to it; Ibn Hibban: we prepared; its parallel is ﴿He settles the believers (tubawwi'u al-mu'minin)﴾ [Al 'Imran 121], ﴿and He settled you on the earth﴾ [al-A'raf 74], and His words ﴿We will surely settle them in lofty chambers of Paradise﴾.

﴿For Abraham, the place of the House﴾: and "place" (makan) is a substance upon which something else can be fixed, just as time is an accident in which something else can occur; and by the House he meant the Ka'bah.

﴿That you do not associate anything with Me﴾: meaning, We commanded him and covenanted with him that he should not associate anything with Me, ﴿and purify My House for those who circumambulate, and those who stand (in prayer), and those who bow and prostrate﴾, meaning those who pray.
