Then theft spread among them, and each person stole from his own side. A man made a door, and 'Umar sent to him: "Have you made a door against the pilgrims of the House of Allah?" He said: "No, I only made it to guard their goods." And this is His words: ﴿equal, the one who dwells there and the visitor﴾.

He said: the visitor there is like the resident; no one has a greater right to a dwelling than another, unless one has preceded to a dwelling. To this view went Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Zayd and Badhan, who said: they are equal in houses and dwellings. The first view is nearer to the truth.

Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan reported to us by my reading to him, saying: Safwan ibn al-Husayn told us, saying:

Abu Muhammad ibn Abi Hatim told us, saying: I heard Abu Isma'il al-Tirmidhi in Makkah in the year 260 say: I heard Ishaq ibn Rahawayh say: I sat with al-Shafi'i in Makkah, and we discussed the renting of houses in Makkah. He permitted it, and I did not permit it. Al-Shafi'i mentioned a hadith and fell silent, and I began on the chapter, reciting it at length; when I finished, I said to a companion of mine from the people of Marw in Persian: "Mard kama li ani hast qariyah bi Marw" (a man, what do I have, is there a village in Marw), and he understood that I had spoken to my companion in a language that disparaged him. He said to me: "Will you debate?" I said: "I came for debate." He said: Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿those who were expelled from their homes﴾ [Al 'Imran 195] — did He attribute the homes to their owners or not to their owners? And the Prophet (ﷺ) said on the day of the Conquest of Makkah: "Whoever closes his door is safe, and whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe. Has 'Aqil left us any houses?" He attributed the house to its owners or not to its owners? And he said to me: "Did 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, buy the prison house from its owner or not from its owner?" When I knew that the proof had been established against me, I stood up.

﴿And whoever intends therein (fihi), in the Sacred Mosque, with deviation, in wrongdoing﴾: that is, deviation by wrongdoing, which is inclining toward injustice; and the ba' in it is extra, like His words: ﴿grows with the oil (tanbutu bi al-duhn)﴾, that is, grows the oil.

Al-Farra' said: I heard a Bedouin from Rabi'ah, and I asked him about something, and he said: "arju bi dhalika," meaning "arju dhalika" (I hope for that).

And a poet said:

In a valley of Yemen, the shit grows at its breast, and at its base with al-markh and al-shabahan.

That is, al-markh. Al-A'sha said:

We guaranteed the provision of our dependents by our spears, between the cauldrons and the bare-ridged sword.

Meaning: our spears guaranteed the provision of our dependents. Another said:

Has it not reached you, while the news spreads, what the she-camels of the Banu Ziyad suffered?

They differed concerning the meaning of the verse. Mujahid and Qatadah said: ﴿whoever intends therein with deviation, in wrongdoing﴾ is shirk, that one worships other than Allah, the Exalted, therein.

Others said: it is making lawful what is forbidden and committing sins therein.

Ibn Mas'ud said: No man intends an evil deed and it is written against him; even if a man in Aden or another land intends to kill a man in Makkah, or intends an evil deed there without doing it, Allah will make him taste the painful punishment.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it is that you kill there one who does not kill you, or wrong one who does not wrong you. This view is the meaning of the saying of al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd.

Ahmad ibn Abi ... reported to us, saying: al-Mughirah ibn 'Amr reported to us, saying: al-Mufaddal ibn Muhammad told us, saying: Muhammad ibn Yusuf told us, saying: Abu Qurrah told us, saying: Sufyan mentioned from Layth, from Mujahid, that he said: Evil deeds are multiplied in Makkah just as good deeds are multiplied.

Ibn Jurayj: it is making lawful the forbidden deliberately. From Habib ibn Abi Thabit: hoarding food in Makkah. Some said: it is everything that was forbidden of speech and action, even the speaker's saying: "No, by Allah," and "Yes, by Allah."

Shu'bah narrated from Mansur, from Mujahid, from Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, that he had two tents, one in the area outside the sanctuary and the other within the sanctuary; if he wished to rebuke his family, he rebuked them in the other one. When he was asked about that, he said: "We used to hear that among deviation therein is that a man says: 'No, by Allah,' and 'Yes, by Allah.'"

﴿And when We settled (wa idh bawwa'na)﴾: we placed it (wa ṭṭa'na). Ibn 'Abbas said: we made it; al-Hasan: we brought down; Muqatil ibn Sulayman: we guided him to it; Ibn Hibban: we prepared; its parallel is ﴿He settles the believers (tubawwi'u al-mu'minin)﴾ [Al 'Imran 121], ﴿and He settled you on the earth﴾ [al-A'raf 74], and His words ﴿We will surely settle them in lofty chambers of Paradise﴾.

﴿For Abraham, the place of the House﴾: and "place" (makan) is a substance upon which something else can be fixed, just as time is an accident in which something else can occur; and by the House he meant the Ka'bah.

﴿That you do not associate anything with Me﴾: meaning, We commanded him and covenanted with him that he should not associate anything with Me, ﴿and purify My House for those who circumambulate, and those who stand (in prayer), and those who bow and prostrate﴾, meaning those who pray.

And command (O Muhammad) ... Meaning: We also charged Ibrahim (peace be upon him) that he should proclaim (adhdhin) (i.e., inform and call out) among the people concerning the Hajj.

Ibrahim said, "O Lord, how would my voice reach (them)?" He said, "The proclamation is incumbent upon you, and the delivery is upon Me." So Ibrahim stood upon the Maqam, and it was said (he stood) on the mountain of Abu Qubays, and he called out: "O people! Your Lord has built a House, so make pilgrimage to it." Allah made that audible to those in the loins of men and the wombs of women, and to all between East and West, land and sea, those whom Allah, glorified is He, had decreed in His knowledge would perform the Hajj until the Day of Resurrection. They responded, "Here I am, O Allah, here I am."

Ibn 'Abbas said: By "the people" in this verse is meant the people of the qiblah (the Muslims). Al-Hasan claimed that the words of the Exalted, ﴿And proclaim among the people the Hajj﴾, are a new statement (kalam mustanaf), and that the one commanded to this proclamation is Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who was ordered to do so during the Farewell Pilgrimage.

﴿They will come to you on foot﴾: the plural of rajil (one on foot), like qa'im and qiyam, and sa'im and siyam.

﴿And upon every lean camel﴾: meaning, and riding. Dhamir is the emaciated camel. The plural form ﴿they will come﴾ (ya'tina) is used because of kull (every), meaning the female camels. ﴿From every deep ravine﴾: a distant path.

I heard Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Faqih say: I heard Abu al-Qasim Bishr ibn Muhammad ibn Yasin al-Qadi say: "I saw in the tawaf an elderly man whom worship had exhausted, his color turned yellow, with a staff in his hand, circling the House while leaning on it. I approached him and began to ask him. He said to me, 'Where are you from?' I said, 'From Khurasan.' He said, 'In what region is Khurasan?' as if he did not know it. I said, 'A region of the eastern lands.' He said, 'How long do you take to cover this journey?' I said, 'Two or three months.' He said, 'Do you not perform Hajj every year, since you are neighbors of this House?' I said to him, 'And how far is it between you and this House?' He said, 'A five-year journey. I left my land when there was no white in my head or beard.' I said, 'By Allah, this is a manifest exertion, a beautiful obedience, and a true love.' He smiled in my face and recited:

Visit the one you love, even if the home is far away
and between you and him are veils and curtains.
Distance should not prevent you from visiting him,
for the lover is always a visitor to the one he desires.
[Al-'Uhud al-Muhammadiyya – al-Sha'rani: 437.]

﴿That they may witness﴾: that they may be present. ﴿Benefits for them﴾: meaning trade. This is from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and it is the narration of Ibn Ruzayn from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: they are the markets.

Mujahid: trade, and what pleases Allah, glorified is He, of the affairs of this world and the Hereafter.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, 'Ata' al-'Awfi, and Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir: pardon and forgiveness.

﴿And mention the name of Allah on known days﴾: meaning the days of Dhu al-Hijjah according to the view of most exegetes. The ﴿counted days﴾ are the days of tashriq (the days after 'Id al-Adha). They were called "counted" (ma'dudat) because they are few. It was said that the ten days are called "known" (ma'lumat) out of eagerness to know them by reckoning, because the time of Hajj is at their end.

Muqatil said: "The known days are the days of tashriq."

Muhammad ibn Ka'b: "The counted and the known are one and the same."

﴿Over what He has provided for them from the cattle of livestock﴾: meaning the offerings (hada') and sacrificial animals (dahaya) of camels, cows, and sheep.

﴿So eat from them﴾: an imperative of permission, not obligation. The exegetes said: He said this because the people of jahiliyyah used to slaughter their offerings and would not eat anything from the meat of their offerings.

﴿And feed the miserable one﴾: meaning the one afflicted (zamin), the poor one who has nothing. ﴿Then let them complete their (state of) unkemptness﴾ (thumma li-yaqdu): the readers differed on these lam's. Some pronounced them with a kasrah to distinguish thumma from waw and fa', and al-Farra' did so because thumma is a separated part of speech, while waw and fa' are like part of the same word. Others pronounced them with a sukun because they are all lam of command. ﴿Their unkemptness (tafath)﴾: "tafath" means:

All the rites of Hajj, according to Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Qurazi and Mujahid said: it is the rites of Hajj, trimming the mustache, plucking the armpit hair, shaving the pubic hair, and cutting the nails.

'Ikrimah: tafath is hair and nails.

Al-Walibi, from Ibn 'Abbas: it is removing the state of ihram: shaving the head, cutting the nails, wearing clothes, and similar things. The original meaning of tafath in the language is filth. The Arabs say to a man whom they find disgusting, "How dirty you are (ma atfathaka)!" meaning, "How filthy you are! How repulsive you are!" Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

Their armpits were clean; they had not been soiled by filth,
and they had removed from themselves lice and nits.
[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 12/50.]

﴿And let them fulfill their vows﴾: Mujahid said: the vow of Hajj and of the offering, and whatever a person vows of something that is part of the Hajj.

﴿And let them circumambulate the Ancient House﴾: meaning the obligatory tawaf, which is the tawaf al-ifadah (the tawaf of return or visitation), performed after the 'Arafat stay, whether on the day of sacrifice or after it. The scholars differed on the meaning of "ancient" (atiq). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, and Qatadah said: it was called ancient because Allah, glorified is He, freed it (a'taqahu) from tyrants who would reach to destroy it. No tyrant ever overpowered it, and no one was empowered over it except those who would venerate and respect it.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Tubba' came intending to demolish the House. When he reached Qudayd, he was struck with paralysis. He called the rabbis, and they said: "This House has a Lord. No one who intends evil toward it is spared from being struck with harm by Him. If you want to be saved from what has befallen you, do not approach it with evil." He said: So he sent a gift to the House, a covering and leather hides, and it was the first thing to be covered. He slaughtered a thousand camels there, pardoned his people, honored them, and kept ties with them. Thus the place was called al-Matabikh (the kitchens) for the cooking of the people; his horses were excellent, so it was named Jiyad for the horses of Tubba'; and Qu'ayqi'an was named for the clatter of weapons when he came from Madinah.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: It was named so because it was never owned (lam yumlak qatt). This is also the narration of 'Ubayd from Mujahid, who said: "The House was named 'ancient' only because no one has any possession in it."

Ibn Zayd said: because it is ancient, and it is the first house placed for the people. It is said: a sword that is atiq (old) or a dinar that is atiq, meaning old. It was also said: because it is noble before Allah, glorified is He. The Arabs say: a horse that is atiq (noble).

﴿That (is so). And whoever honors the sacred rites of Allah﴾, by avoiding His disobedience, ﴿it is better for him in the sight of his Lord﴾.

Ibn Zayd said: The sacred things (hurumat) are al-Mash'ar al-Haram, the Sacred House, the Sacred Mosque, and the Sacred City. It was also said: they are the rites (manasik).

﴿And lawful to you are the cattle (an'am)﴾ to eat when you have slaughtered them, ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ in the Qur'an, which is His saying: ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion and blood﴾ [5:3] to the end of the verse, and His saying: ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾ [6:121]. It was also said: ﴿And lawful to you are the cattle﴾ during your state of ihram, ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ concerning game, for it is forbidden during the state of ihram.

﴿So avoid the filth of idols﴾: meaning worshipping them, because all idols are filth.

﴿And avoid the speech of falsehood﴾: meaning lying and slander.

Ayman ibn Hurrayn said: The Prophet (ﷺ) gave a sermon and said: "O people! The false testimony has been made equal to associating partners with Allah," then he recited this verse. [5] [Musnad Ahmad: 4/178.]

Some of them said: it is the statement of the polytheists in their talbiyah: "Here I am, You have no partner, except a partner who is Yours; You own him and what he owns."

﴿Ḥunafa'﴾: upright, sincere, devoted to Allah. It was also said: pilgrims. ﴿Not associating anything with Him﴾. ﴿And whoever associates with Allah, it is as if he had fallen from the sky﴾, meaning he dropped to the earth, ﴿and the birds snatch him away﴾. The words khatf and ikhtitaf mean taking something swiftly. The people of Madinah read ﴿fatakhattafuhu﴾ with a fatha on the kha' and shaddah on the ta', meaning tatakhattafuhu, and they assimilated the letters. The reading of the general readers is confirmed by His saying: ﴿except one who snatches a snatch﴾ [37:10].

﴿Or the wind carries him off to a distant place﴾: meaning far away.

The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: The condition of the polytheist is compared to that of one who falls, in that he possesses no benefit for himself and no removal of harm on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Hasan said: The deeds of the disbelievers are compared to this state, in that they are swept away and nullified, so they are unable to achieve anything from them.

﴿That (is so)﴾, meaning what I have mentioned of avoiding filth and falsehood and glorifying the rites of Allah, ﴿is from the piety of hearts﴾. This is the meaning and arrangement of the verse. The rites of Allah (sha'a'ir Allah) are the offerings (hady) and the camels (budn). The root is from ish'ar (marking), which is announcing them so that they may be recognized as offerings, and they are named after it. Glorifying them means deeming them great, finding them beautiful, and choosing them to be fat.

﴿For you in them﴾, meaning in the offerings, ﴿are benefits﴾. It was said: that their owner names them a budnah or hady, marks them, and garlands them, and you may benefit from their milk, wool, and fur, and ride upon their backs. ﴿Until a specified term﴾: which is that once he names it an offering and makes it obligatory, then when he does so, he has no benefit from them. This is the view of Mujahid, 'Ata', al-Dahhak, and Qatadah, and the narration of Muqsim from Ibn 'Abbas. It was also said: the meaning is that in these offerings there are benefits for you after they are brought forth and named as offerings, by riding them when you need to, and drinking their milk if you are compelled to, ﴿until a specified term﴾, meaning until they are slaughtered. This is the view of 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah.

Some of them said: By the rites (sha'a'ir) he meant the manasik and the sacred sites of Makkah. The meaning of the verse: ﴿For you in them are benefits﴾ through trade and markets, ﴿until a specified term﴾, which is leaving Makkah. This is the narration of Abu Dharr from Ibn 'Abbas.

Some of them said: ﴿For you in them are benefits﴾ through reward and recompense in performing the rites and establishing the rites of Hajj, ﴿until a specified term﴾, which is the end of the days of Hajj.

﴿Then their place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House﴾: meaning their place of slaughter is near the Ancient House, that is, the whole land of the Haram. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿So let them not approach the Sacred Mosque after this year﴾ [9:28], meaning the entire Haram. Those who said the rites (sha'a'ir) mean the manasik said the meaning of the verse is: ﴿Then their place of release from their ihram is at the Ancient House﴾, that they circumambulate it with the tawaf of visitation on the day of sacrifice after completing the rites.

﴿And for every community﴾, meaning every believing congregation that preceded you, ﴿We have appointed a rite (mansak)﴾. The readers differed about it. The people of Kufa, except 'Asim, read it with a kasrah on the sin in both instances, as an ism (noun), like majlis and mut tali', meaning a place of sacrifice, a site of offering. The others read it with a fatha on the sin in both instances, as a masdar (verbal noun), like mudkhal and makhraj, meaning the shedding of blood and the slaughter of offerings.

﴿That they may mention the name of Allah over what He has provided for them from the cattle of livestock﴾ at the time of their slaughter and sacrifice. The phrase "cattle of livestock" is specified because among beasts there are some that are not livestock, such as horses, mules, and donkeys. Beasts (bahaʾim) is so named because they cannot speak.

﴿Your God is one God, so submit to Him. And give good tidings to the humble (mukhbitin)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: the humble, the modest. Mujahid: those at peace with Allah, glorified is He. Al-Akhfash: the humbled. Ibn Jarir: the submissive. 'Amr ibn Aws: those who do not wrong, and if they are wronged, they do not seek retribution.

﴿Those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and those who are patient over what befalls them, and those who establish prayer, and from what We have provided them they spend﴾. ﴿And the camels (budn)﴾, meaning the large, massive-bodied camels. It is read with both light and heavy pronunciation; its singular is budnah, like tamrah and tamr, khashabah and khashab, and bādin like fāriḥ and fārah. Budn is the large of everything, and from it comes the saying about Imru' al-Qays ibn al-Nu'man, lord of Khawarnaq and Sadir: "al-Budn," because of his bulk. One says the man became budn (bulky) when he grew large. When he became heavy and slack, it is said: badan, yubaddin tabdinan.

'Ata' and al-Suddi said: al-budn: the camels and the cows.

﴿We have made them for you among the rites of Allah﴾, meaning the markers of His religion when they are marked. ﴿For you in them is good﴾: benefit in this world, and reward in the Hereafter. ﴿So mention the name of Allah over them﴾ at the time of their slaughter. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is to say, "Allahu akbar, la ilaha illa Allah, wa Allahu akbar, Allahumma minka wa laka."

﴿Standing in rows (sawaff)﴾: meaning standing on three legs, with their feet arranged and one of their forelegs bound, and the left foreleg tied, so the animal is slaughtered in that position.

Yala ibn 'Ata' narrated from Yahya ibn Salim, who said: "I saw Ibn 'Umar slaughtering his camel, and he said, 'Standing in rows, as Allah, glorified is He, said.' He slaughtered it while it was standing and tied, one of its forelegs bound."

Mujahid said: "Sawaff" means when its left hind leg is tied, and it stands on three legs, and it is slaughtered in that manner.

Ibn Mas'ud read: ﴿sawafin﴾, which means those tied by one foreleg, and it stands on three legs and is slaughtered; it is like sawaff. Ubayy read: ﴿sawafi﴾, and likewise Mujahid and Zayd ibn Aslam with the ya', meaning pure and sincere for Allah, glorified is He, with no partner in them, as the polytheists used to do.

﴿So when they have fallen on their sides (wajabat junubuha)﴾, meaning when they fall after slaughter and their sides come to rest on the ground.

Ibn Zayd said: "When they have died." The root meaning of wujub is falling. It is said: "Wajabat al-shams" when the sun sets, and "wajaba al-fi'l" when the action that must be performed occurs.

﴿Then eat from them﴾: an imperative of permission and concession, like His saying: ﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾ [5:2], and His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse in the land﴾ [62:10].

﴿And feed the contented (qani') and the beggar (mu'tarr)﴾. They differed about their meanings. Al-'Awfi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and Layth from Mujahid, that al-qani' is the one who is content with what is given to him and satisfied with what he has, and does not ask; and al-mu'tarr is the one who passes by you and presents himself to you without asking.

'Ikrimah, Ibn Maysam, and Qatadah: al-qani' is the one who is modest, sitting in his house, and al-mu'tarr is the beggar who comes to you and asks you. This is the narration of al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas. According to these interpretations, al-qani' is from qana'ah, which is contentment, modesty, and abstaining from asking.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Kalbi: al-qani' is the one who asks you, and al-mu'tarr is the one who presents himself to you and shows you his need without asking. According to this view, al-qani' is from qunu', which is asking. Al-Shammakh said:

The wealth of a man sustains him, so he becomes rich,
and his poverty is more chaste than begging.

Labid said:

My lord gave me when I was in poverty,
when he said, "Look at my need and my begging."

Zayd ibn Aslam said: al-qani' is the poor man who goes around asking, and al-mu'tarr is the visiting friend who visits to partake of the budn.

Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: al-qani' is the one who is greedy; al-mu'tarr is the one who comes for the budn, whether rich or poor.

Ibn Zayd: al-qani' is the needy one, and al-mu'tarr is the one who visits the people for their meat, and is not poor and does not have a sacrifice of his own; he comes to the people for the sake of their meat.

Al-Hasan read: ﴿wal-mu'tari﴾, which is like al-mu'tarr. It is said: 'araka and i'taraka when he comes to you seeking your favor.

﴿Thus We have subjected them to you, that you may be grateful﴾.

﴿It is not their meat that reaches Allah, nor their blood, but it is piety from you that reaches Him﴾. This is because the people of jahiliyyah, when they slaughtered the budn, would smear the walls of the Ka'bah with their blood. So Allah, glorified is He, revealed: ﴿It is not their meat that reaches Allah﴾, meaning does not reach Allah, ﴿nor their blood﴾.

﴿But it is piety from you that reaches Him﴾, meaning the intention, sincerity, and what is intended for the Face of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. Ya'qub read ﴿tanal﴾ and ﴿tanaluhu﴾ with the ta', and others with the ya'.

﴿Thus﴾, meaning in this way, ﴿He has subjected them﴾, meaning the budn, ﴿to you, that you may glorify Allah for having guided you﴾ to the markers of His religion and the rites of His Hajj. This means that you say, "Allahu akbar for what He has guided us to, and al-hamdu lillah for what He has tried us with and granted us."

And command (O Muhammad) ... Meaning: We also charged Ibrahim (peace be upon him) that he should proclaim (adhdhin) (i.e., inform and call out) among the people concerning the Hajj.

Ibrahim said, "O Lord, how would my voice reach (them)?" He said, "The proclamation is incumbent upon you, and the delivery is upon Me." So Ibrahim stood upon the Maqam, and it was said (he stood) on the mountain of Abu Qubays, and he called out: "O people! Your Lord has built a House, so make pilgrimage to it." Allah made that audible to those in the loins of men and the wombs of women, and to all between East and West, land and sea, those whom Allah, glorified is He, had decreed in His knowledge would perform the Hajj until the Day of Resurrection. They responded, "Here I am, O Allah, here I am."

Ibn 'Abbas said: By "the people" in this verse is meant the people of the qiblah (the Muslims). Al-Hasan claimed that the words of the Exalted, ﴿And proclaim among the people the Hajj﴾, are a new statement (kalam mustanaf), and that the one commanded to this proclamation is Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who was ordered to do so during the Farewell Pilgrimage.

﴿They will come to you on foot﴾: the plural of rajil (one on foot), like qa'im and qiyam, and sa'im and siyam.

﴿And upon every lean camel﴾: meaning, and riding. Dhamir is the emaciated camel. The plural form ﴿they will come﴾ (ya'tina) is used because of kull (every), meaning the female camels. ﴿From every deep ravine﴾: a distant path.

I heard Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Faqih say: I heard Abu al-Qasim Bishr ibn Muhammad ibn Yasin al-Qadi say: "I saw in the tawaf an elderly man whom worship had exhausted, his color turned yellow, with a staff in his hand, circling the House while leaning on it. I approached him and began to ask him. He said to me, 'Where are you from?' I said, 'From Khurasan.' He said, 'In what region is Khurasan?' as if he did not know it. I said, 'A region of the eastern lands.' He said, 'How long do you take to cover this journey?' I said, 'Two or three months.' He said, 'Do you not perform Hajj every year, since you are neighbors of this House?' I said to him, 'And how far is it between you and this House?' He said, 'A five-year journey. I left my land when there was no white in my head or beard.' I said, 'By Allah, this is a manifest exertion, a beautiful obedience, and a true love.' He smiled in my face and recited:

Visit the one you love, even if the home is far away
and between you and him are veils and curtains.
Distance should not prevent you from visiting him,
for the lover is always a visitor to the one he desires.
[Al-'Uhud al-Muhammadiyya – al-Sha'rani: 437.]

﴿That they may witness﴾: that they may be present. ﴿Benefits for them﴾: meaning trade. This is from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and it is the narration of Ibn Ruzayn from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: they are the markets.

Mujahid: trade, and what pleases Allah, glorified is He, of the affairs of this world and the Hereafter.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, 'Ata' al-'Awfi, and Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir: pardon and forgiveness.

﴿And mention the name of Allah on known days﴾: meaning the days of Dhu al-Hijjah according to the view of most exegetes. The ﴿counted days﴾ are the days of tashriq (the days after 'Id al-Adha). They were called "counted" (ma'dudat) because they are few. It was said that the ten days are called "known" (ma'lumat) out of eagerness to know them by reckoning, because the time of Hajj is at their end.

Muqatil said: "The known days are the days of tashriq."

Muhammad ibn Ka'b: "The counted and the known are one and the same."

﴿Over what He has provided for them from the cattle of livestock﴾: meaning the offerings (hada') and sacrificial animals (dahaya) of camels, cows, and sheep.

﴿So eat from them﴾: an imperative of permission, not obligation. The exegetes said: He said this because the people of jahiliyyah used to slaughter their offerings and would not eat anything from the meat of their offerings.

﴿And feed the miserable one﴾: meaning the one afflicted (zamin), the poor one who has nothing. ﴿Then let them complete their (state of) unkemptness﴾ (thumma li-yaqdu): the readers differed on these lam's. Some pronounced them with a kasrah to distinguish thumma from waw and fa', and al-Farra' did so because thumma is a separated part of speech, while waw and fa' are like part of the same word. Others pronounced them with a sukun because they are all lam of command. ﴿Their unkemptness (tafath)﴾: "tafath" means:

All the rites of Hajj, according to Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Qurazi and Mujahid said: it is the rites of Hajj, trimming the mustache, plucking the armpit hair, shaving the pubic hair, and cutting the nails.

'Ikrimah: tafath is hair and nails.

Al-Walibi, from Ibn 'Abbas: it is removing the state of ihram: shaving the head, cutting the nails, wearing clothes, and similar things. The original meaning of tafath in the language is filth. The Arabs say to a man whom they find disgusting, "How dirty you are (ma atfathaka)!" meaning, "How filthy you are! How repulsive you are!" Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

Their armpits were clean; they had not been soiled by filth,
and they had removed from themselves lice and nits.
[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 12/50.]

﴿And let them fulfill their vows﴾: Mujahid said: the vow of Hajj and of the offering, and whatever a person vows of something that is part of the Hajj.

﴿And let them circumambulate the Ancient House﴾: meaning the obligatory tawaf, which is the tawaf al-ifadah (the tawaf of return or visitation), performed after the 'Arafat stay, whether on the day of sacrifice or after it. The scholars differed on the meaning of "ancient" (atiq). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, and Qatadah said: it was called ancient because Allah, glorified is He, freed it (a'taqahu) from tyrants who would reach to destroy it. No tyrant ever overpowered it, and no one was empowered over it except those who would venerate and respect it.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Tubba' came intending to demolish the House. When he reached Qudayd, he was struck with paralysis. He called the rabbis, and they said: "This House has a Lord. No one who intends evil toward it is spared from being struck with harm by Him. If you want to be saved from what has befallen you, do not approach it with evil." He said: So he sent a gift to the House, a covering and leather hides, and it was the first thing to be covered. He slaughtered a thousand camels there, pardoned his people, honored them, and kept ties with them. Thus the place was called al-Matabikh (the kitchens) for the cooking of the people; his horses were excellent, so it was named Jiyad for the horses of Tubba'; and Qu'ayqi'an was named for the clatter of weapons when he came from Madinah.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: It was named so because it was never owned (lam yumlak qatt). This is also the narration of 'Ubayd from Mujahid, who said: "The House was named 'ancient' only because no one has any possession in it."

Ibn Zayd said: because it is ancient, and it is the first house placed for the people. It is said: a sword that is atiq (old) or a dinar that is atiq, meaning old. It was also said: because it is noble before Allah, glorified is He. The Arabs say: a horse that is atiq (noble).

﴿That (is so). And whoever honors the sacred rites of Allah﴾, by avoiding His disobedience, ﴿it is better for him in the sight of his Lord﴾.

Ibn Zayd said: The sacred things (hurumat) are al-Mash'ar al-Haram, the Sacred House, the Sacred Mosque, and the Sacred City. It was also said: they are the rites (manasik).

﴿And lawful to you are the cattle (an'am)﴾ to eat when you have slaughtered them, ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ in the Qur'an, which is His saying: ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion and blood﴾ [5:3] to the end of the verse, and His saying: ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾ [6:121]. It was also said: ﴿And lawful to you are the cattle﴾ during your state of ihram, ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ concerning game, for it is forbidden during the state of ihram.

﴿So avoid the filth of idols﴾: meaning worshipping them, because all idols are filth.

﴿And avoid the speech of falsehood﴾: meaning lying and slander.

Ayman ibn Hurrayn said: The Prophet (ﷺ) gave a sermon and said: "O people! The false testimony has been made equal to associating partners with Allah," then he recited this verse. [5] [Musnad Ahmad: 4/178.]

Some of them said: it is the statement of the polytheists in their talbiyah: "Here I am, You have no partner, except a partner who is Yours; You own him and what he owns."

﴿Ḥunafa'﴾: upright, sincere, devoted to Allah. It was also said: pilgrims. ﴿Not associating anything with Him﴾. ﴿And whoever associates with Allah, it is as if he had fallen from the sky﴾, meaning he dropped to the earth, ﴿and the birds snatch him away﴾. The words khatf and ikhtitaf mean taking something swiftly. The people of Madinah read ﴿fatakhattafuhu﴾ with a fatha on the kha' and shaddah on the ta', meaning tatakhattafuhu, and they assimilated the letters. The reading of the general readers is confirmed by His saying: ﴿except one who snatches a snatch﴾ [37:10].

﴿Or the wind carries him off to a distant place﴾: meaning far away.

The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: The condition of the polytheist is compared to that of one who falls, in that he possesses no benefit for himself and no removal of harm on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Hasan said: The deeds of the disbelievers are compared to this state, in that they are swept away and nullified, so they are unable to achieve anything from them.

﴿That (is so)﴾, meaning what I have mentioned of avoiding filth and falsehood and glorifying the rites of Allah, ﴿is from the piety of hearts﴾. This is the meaning and arrangement of the verse. The rites of Allah (sha'a'ir Allah) are the offerings (hady) and the camels (budn). The root is from ish'ar (marking), which is announcing them so that they may be recognized as offerings, and they are named after it. Glorifying them means deeming them great, finding them beautiful, and choosing them to be fat.

﴿For you in them﴾, meaning in the offerings, ﴿are benefits﴾. It was said: that their owner names them a budnah or hady, marks them, and garlands them, and you may benefit from their milk, wool, and fur, and ride upon their backs. ﴿Until a specified term﴾: which is that once he names it an offering and makes it obligatory, then when he does so, he has no benefit from them. This is the view of Mujahid, 'Ata', al-Dahhak, and Qatadah, and the narration of Muqsim from Ibn 'Abbas. It was also said: the meaning is that in these offerings there are benefits for you after they are brought forth and named as offerings, by riding them when you need to, and drinking their milk if you are compelled to, ﴿until a specified term﴾, meaning until they are slaughtered. This is the view of 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah.

Some of them said: By the rites (sha'a'ir) he meant the manasik and the sacred sites of Makkah. The meaning of the verse: ﴿For you in them are benefits﴾ through trade and markets, ﴿until a specified term﴾, which is leaving Makkah. This is the narration of Abu Dharr from Ibn 'Abbas.

Some of them said: ﴿For you in them are benefits﴾ through reward and recompense in performing the rites and establishing the rites of Hajj, ﴿until a specified term﴾, which is the end of the days of Hajj.

﴿Then their place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House﴾: meaning their place of slaughter is near the Ancient House, that is, the whole land of the Haram. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿So let them not approach the Sacred Mosque after this year﴾ [9:28], meaning the entire Haram. Those who said the rites (sha'a'ir) mean the manasik said the meaning of the verse is: ﴿Then their place of release from their ihram is at the Ancient House﴾, that they circumambulate it with the tawaf of visitation on the day of sacrifice after completing the rites.

﴿And for every community﴾, meaning every believing congregation that preceded you, ﴿We have appointed a rite (mansak)﴾. The readers differed about it. The people of Kufa, except 'Asim, read it with a kasrah on the sin in both instances, as an ism (noun), like majlis and mut tali', meaning a place of sacrifice, a site of offering. The others read it with a fatha on the sin in both instances, as a masdar (verbal noun), like mudkhal and makhraj, meaning the shedding of blood and the slaughter of offerings.

﴿That they may mention the name of Allah over what He has provided for them from the cattle of livestock﴾ at the time of their slaughter and sacrifice. The phrase "cattle of livestock" is specified because among beasts there are some that are not livestock, such as horses, mules, and donkeys. Beasts (bahaʾim) is so named because they cannot speak.

﴿Your God is one God, so submit to Him. And give good tidings to the humble (mukhbitin)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: the humble, the modest. Mujahid: those at peace with Allah, glorified is He. Al-Akhfash: the humbled. Ibn Jarir: the submissive. 'Amr ibn Aws: those who do not wrong, and if they are wronged, they do not seek retribution.

﴿Those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and those who are patient over what befalls them, and those who establish prayer, and from what We have provided them they spend﴾. ﴿And the camels (budn)﴾, meaning the large, massive-bodied camels. It is read with both light and heavy pronunciation; its singular is budnah, like tamrah and tamr, khashabah and khashab, and bādin like fāriḥ and fārah. Budn is the large of everything, and from it comes the saying about Imru' al-Qays ibn al-Nu'man, lord of Khawarnaq and Sadir: "al-Budn," because of his bulk. One says the man became budn (bulky) when he grew large. When he became heavy and slack, it is said: badan, yubaddin tabdinan.

'Ata' and al-Suddi said: al-budn: the camels and the cows.

﴿We have made them for you among the rites of Allah﴾, meaning the markers of His religion when they are marked. ﴿For you in them is good﴾: benefit in this world, and reward in the Hereafter. ﴿So mention the name of Allah over them﴾ at the time of their slaughter. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is to say, "Allahu akbar, la ilaha illa Allah, wa Allahu akbar, Allahumma minka wa laka."

﴿Standing in rows (sawaff)﴾: meaning standing on three legs, with their feet arranged and one of their forelegs bound, and the left foreleg tied, so the animal is slaughtered in that position.

Yala ibn 'Ata' narrated from Yahya ibn Salim, who said: "I saw Ibn 'Umar slaughtering his camel, and he said, 'Standing in rows, as Allah, glorified is He, said.' He slaughtered it while it was standing and tied, one of its forelegs bound."

Mujahid said: "Sawaff" means when its left hind leg is tied, and it stands on three legs, and it is slaughtered in that manner.

Ibn Mas'ud read: ﴿sawafin﴾, which means those tied by one foreleg, and it stands on three legs and is slaughtered; it is like sawaff. Ubayy read: ﴿sawafi﴾, and likewise Mujahid and Zayd ibn Aslam with the ya', meaning pure and sincere for Allah, glorified is He, with no partner in them, as the polytheists used to do.

﴿So when they have fallen on their sides (wajabat junubuha)﴾, meaning when they fall after slaughter and their sides come to rest on the ground.

Ibn Zayd said: "When they have died." The root meaning of wujub is falling. It is said: "Wajabat al-shams" when the sun sets, and "wajaba al-fi'l" when the action that must be performed occurs.

﴿Then eat from them﴾: an imperative of permission and concession, like His saying: ﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾ [5:2], and His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse in the land﴾ [62:10].

Al-'Awfi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and Layth from Mujahid, that al-qani' is the one who is content with what is given to him and satisfied with what he has, and does not ask; and al-mu'tarr is the one who passes by you and presents himself to you without asking.

'Ikrimah, Ibn Maysam, and Qatadah: al-qani' is the one who is modest, sitting in his house, and al-mu'tarr is the beggar who comes to you and asks you. This is the narration of al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas. According to these interpretations, al-qani' is from qana'ah, which is contentment, modesty, and abstaining from asking.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Kalbi: al-qani' is the one who asks you, and al-mu'tarr is the one who presents himself to you and shows you his need without asking. According to this view, al-qani' is from qunu', which is asking. Al-Shammakh said:

The wealth of a man sustains him, so he becomes rich,
and his poverty is more chaste than begging.

Labid said:

My lord gave me when I was in poverty,
when he said, "Look at my need and my begging."

Zayd ibn Aslam said: al-qani' is the poor man who goes around asking, and al-mu'tarr is the visiting friend who visits to partake of the budn.

Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: al-qani' is the one who is greedy; al-mu'tarr is the one who comes for the budn, whether rich or poor.

Ibn Zayd: al-qani' is the needy one, and al-mu'tarr is the one who visits the people for their meat, and is not poor and does not have a sacrifice of his own; he comes to the people for the sake of their meat.

Al-Hasan read: ﴿wal-mu'tari﴾, which is like al-mu'tarr. It is said: 'araka and i'taraka when he comes to you seeking your favor.

﴿Thus We have subjected them to you, that you may be grateful﴾.

﴿It is not their meat that reaches Allah, nor their blood, but it is piety from you that reaches Him﴾. This is because the people of jahiliyyah, when they slaughtered the budn, would smear the walls of the Ka'bah with their blood. So Allah, glorified is He, revealed: ﴿It is not their meat that reaches Allah﴾, meaning does not reach Allah, ﴿nor their blood﴾.

﴿But it is piety from you that reaches Him﴾, meaning the intention, sincerity, and what is intended for the Face of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. Ya'qub read ﴿tanal﴾ and ﴿tanaluhu﴾ with the ta', and others with the ya'.

﴿Thus﴾, meaning in this way, ﴿He has subjected them﴾, meaning the budn, ﴿to you, that you may glorify Allah for having guided you﴾ to the markers of His religion and the rites of His Hajj. This means that you say, "Allahu akbar for what He has guided us to, and al-hamdu lillah for what He has tried us with and granted us."

And command (O Muhammad) ... Meaning: We also charged Ibrahim (peace be upon him) that he should proclaim (adhdhin) (i.e., inform and call out) among the people concerning the Hajj.

Ibrahim said, "O Lord, how would my voice reach (them)?" He said, "The proclamation is incumbent upon you, and the delivery is upon Me." So Ibrahim stood upon the Maqam, and it was said (he stood) on the mountain of Abu Qubays, and he called out: "O people! Your Lord has built a House, so make pilgrimage to it." Allah made that audible to those in the loins of men and the wombs of women, and to all between East and West, land and sea, those whom Allah, glorified is He, had decreed in His knowledge would perform the Hajj until the Day of Resurrection. They responded, "Here I am, O Allah, here I am."

Ibn 'Abbas said: By "the people" in this verse is meant the people of the qiblah (the Muslims). Al-Hasan claimed that the words of the Exalted, ﴿And proclaim among the people the Hajj﴾, are a new statement (kalam mustanaf), and that the one commanded to this proclamation is Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who was ordered to do so during the Farewell Pilgrimage.

﴿They will come to you on foot﴾: the plural of rajil (one on foot), like qa'im and qiyam, and sa'im and siyam.

﴿And upon every lean camel﴾: meaning, and riding. Dhamir is the emaciated camel. The plural form ﴿they will come﴾ (ya'tina) is used because of kull (every), meaning the female camels. ﴿From every deep ravine﴾: a distant path.

I heard Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Faqih say: I heard Abu al-Qasim Bishr ibn Muhammad ibn Yasin al-Qadi say: "I saw in the tawaf an elderly man whom worship had exhausted, his color turned yellow, with a staff in his hand, circling the House while leaning on it. I approached him and began to ask him. He said to me, 'Where are you from?' I said, 'From Khurasan.' He said, 'In what region is Khurasan?' as if he did not know it. I said, 'A region of the eastern lands.' He said, 'How long do you take to cover this journey?' I said, 'Two or three months.' He said, 'Do you not perform Hajj every year, since you are neighbors of this House?' I said to him, 'And how far is it between you and this House?' He said, 'A five-year journey. I left my land when there was no white in my head or beard.' I said, 'By Allah, this is a manifest exertion, a beautiful obedience, and a true love.' He smiled in my face and recited:

Visit the one you love, even if the home is far away
and between you and him are veils and curtains.
Distance should not prevent you from visiting him,
for the lover is always a visitor to the one he desires.
[Al-'Uhud al-Muhammadiyya – al-Sha'rani: 437.]

This is the view of Mujahid, 'Ata', al-Dahhak, and Qatadah, and the narration of Muqsim from Ibn 'Abbas. It was also said: the meaning is that in these offerings there are benefits for you after they are brought forth and named as offerings, by riding them when you need to, and drinking their milk if you are compelled to, ﴿until a specified term﴾, meaning until they are slaughtered. This is the view of 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah.

Some of them said: By the rites (sha'a'ir) he meant the manasik and the sacred sites of Makkah. The meaning of the verse: ﴿For you in them are benefits﴾ through trade and markets, ﴿until a specified term﴾, which is leaving Makkah. This is the narration of Abu Dharr from Ibn 'Abbas.

Some of them said: ﴿For you in them are benefits﴾ through reward and recompense in performing the rites and establishing the rites of Hajj, ﴿until a specified term﴾, which is the end of the days of Hajj.

﴿Then their place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House﴾: meaning their place of slaughter is near the Ancient House, that is, the whole land of the Haram. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿So let them not approach the Sacred Mosque after this year﴾ [9:28], meaning the entire Haram. Those who said the rites (sha'a'ir) mean the manasik said the meaning of the verse is: ﴿Then their place of release from their ihram is at the Ancient House﴾, that they circumambulate it with the tawaf of visitation on the day of sacrifice after completing the rites.

﴿And for every community﴾, meaning every believing congregation that preceded you, ﴿We have appointed a rite (mansak)﴾. The readers differed about it. The people of Kufa, except 'Asim, read it with a kasrah on the sin in both instances, as an ism (noun), like majlis and mut tali', meaning a place of sacrifice, a site of offering. The others read it with a fatha on the sin in both instances, as a masdar (verbal noun), like mudkhal and makhraj, meaning the shedding of blood and the slaughter of offerings.

﴿That they may mention the name of Allah over what He has provided for them from the cattle of livestock﴾ at the time of their slaughter and sacrifice. The phrase "cattle of livestock" is specified because among beasts there are some that are not livestock, such as horses, mules, and donkeys. Beasts (bahaʾim) is so named because they cannot speak.

﴿Your God is one God, so submit to Him. And give good tidings to the humble (mukhbitin)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: the humble, the modest. Mujahid: those at peace with Allah, glorified is He. Al-Akhfash: the humbled. Ibn Jarir: the submissive. 'Amr ibn Aws: those who do not wrong, and if they are wronged, they do not seek retribution.

﴿Those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and those who are patient over what befalls them, and those who establish prayer, and from what We have provided them they spend﴾. ﴿And the camels (budn)﴾, meaning the large, massive-bodied camels. It is read with both light and heavy pronunciation; its singular is budnah, like tamrah and tamr, khashabah and khashab, and bādin like fāriḥ and fārah. Budn is the large of everything, and from it comes the saying about Imru' al-Qays ibn al-Nu'man, lord of Khawarnaq and Sadir: "al-Budn," because of his bulk. One says the man became budn (bulky) when he grew large. When he became heavy and slack, it is said: badan, yubaddin tabdinan.

'Ata' and al-Suddi said: al-budn: the camels and the cows.

﴿We have made them for you among the rites of Allah﴾, meaning the markers of His religion when they are marked. ﴿For you in them is good﴾: benefit in this world, and reward in the Hereafter. ﴿So mention the name of Allah over them﴾ at the time of their slaughter. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is to say, "Allahu akbar, la ilaha illa Allah, wa Allahu akbar, Allahumma minka wa laka."

﴿Standing in rows (sawaff)﴾: meaning standing on three legs, with their feet arranged and one of their forelegs bound, and the left foreleg tied, so the animal is slaughtered in that position.

Yala ibn 'Ata' narrated from Yahya ibn Salim, who said: "I saw Ibn 'Umar slaughtering his camel, and he said, 'Standing in rows, as Allah, glorified is He, said.' He slaughtered it while it was standing and tied, one of its forelegs bound."

Mujahid said: "Sawaff" means when its left hind leg is tied, and it stands on three legs, and it is slaughtered in that manner.

Ibn Mas'ud read: ﴿sawafin﴾, which means those tied by one foreleg, and it stands on three legs and is slaughtered; it is like sawaff. Ubayy read: ﴿sawafi﴾, and likewise Mujahid and Zayd ibn Aslam with the ya', meaning pure and sincere for Allah, glorified is He, with no partner in them, as the polytheists used to do.

﴿So when they have fallen on their sides (wajabat junubuha)﴾, meaning when they fall after slaughter and their sides come to rest on the ground.

Ibn Zayd said: "When they have died." The root meaning of wujub is falling. It is said: "Wajabat al-shams" when the sun sets, and "wajaba al-fi'l" when the action that must be performed occurs.

﴿Then eat from them﴾: an imperative of permission and concession, like His saying: ﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾ [5:2], and His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse in the land﴾ [62:10].

﴿And feed the contented (qani') and the beggar (mu'tarr)﴾. They differed about their meanings. Al-'Awfi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and Layth from Mujahid, that al-qani' is the one who is content with what is given to him and satisfied with what he has, and does not ask; and al-mu'tarr is the one who passes by you and presents himself to you without asking.

'Ikrimah, Ibn Maysam, and Qatadah: al-qani' is the one who is modest, sitting in his house, and al-mu'tarr is the beggar who comes to you and asks you. This is the narration of al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas. According to these interpretations, al-qani' is from qana'ah, which is contentment, modesty, and abstaining from asking.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Kalbi: al-qani' is the one who asks you, and al-mu'tarr is the one who presents himself to you and shows you his need without asking. According to this view, al-qani' is from qunu', which is asking. Al-Shammakh said:

The wealth of a man sustains him, so he becomes rich,
and his poverty is more chaste than begging.

Labid said:

My lord gave me when I was in poverty,
when he said, "Look at my need and my begging."

Zayd ibn Aslam said: al-qani' is the poor man who goes around asking, and al-mu'tarr is the visiting friend who visits to partake of the budn.

Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: al-qani' is the one who is greedy; al-mu'tarr is the one who comes for the budn, whether rich or poor.

Ibn Zayd: al-qani' is the needy one, and al-mu'tarr is the one who visits the people for their meat, and is not poor and does not have a sacrifice of his own; he comes to the people for the sake of their meat.

Al-Hasan read: ﴿wal-mu'tari﴾, which is like al-mu'tarr. It is said: 'araka and i'taraka when he comes to you seeking your favor.

﴿Thus We have subjected them to you, that you may be grateful﴾.

﴿It is not their meat that reaches Allah, nor their blood, but it is piety from you that reaches Him﴾. This is because the people of jahiliyyah, when they slaughtered the budn, would smear the walls of the Ka'bah with their blood. So Allah, glorified is He, revealed: ﴿It is not their meat that reaches Allah﴾, meaning does not reach Allah, ﴿nor their blood﴾.

﴿But it is piety from you that reaches Him﴾, meaning the intention, sincerity, and what is intended for the Face of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. Ya'qub read ﴿tanal﴾ and ﴿tanaluhu﴾ with the ta', and others with the ya'.

﴿Thus﴾, meaning in this way, ﴿He has subjected them﴾, meaning the budn, ﴿to you, that you may glorify Allah for having guided you﴾ to the markers of His religion and the rites of His Hajj. This means that you say, "Allahu akbar for what He has guided us to, and al-hamdu lillah for what He has tried us with and granted us."

And command (O Muhammad) ... Meaning: We also charged Ibrahim (peace be upon him) that he should proclaim (adhdhin) (i.e., inform and call out) among the people concerning the Hajj.

Ibrahim said, "O Lord, how would my voice reach (them)?" He said, "The proclamation is incumbent upon you, and the delivery is upon Me." So Ibrahim stood upon the Maqam, and it was said (he stood) on the mountain of Abu Qubays, and he called out: "O people! Your Lord has built a House, so make pilgrimage to it." Allah made that audible to those in the loins of men and the wombs of women, and to all between East and West, land and sea, those whom Allah, glorified is He, had decreed in His knowledge would perform the Hajj until the Day of Resurrection. They responded, "Here I am, O Allah, here I am."

Ibn 'Abbas said: By "the people" in this verse is meant the people of the qiblah (the Muslims). Al-Hasan claimed that the words of the Exalted, ﴿And proclaim among the people the Hajj﴾, are a new statement (kalam mustanaf), and that the one commanded to this proclamation is Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who was ordered to do so during the Farewell Pilgrimage.

﴿They will come to you on foot﴾: the plural of rajil (one on foot), like qa'im and qiyam, and sa'im and siyam.

﴿And upon every lean camel﴾: meaning, and riding. Dhamir is the emaciated camel. The plural form ﴿they will come﴾ (ya'tina) is used because of kull (every), meaning the female camels. ﴿From every deep ravine﴾: a distant path.

I heard Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Faqih say: I heard Abu al-Qasim Bishr ibn Muhammad ibn Yasin al-Qadi say: "I saw in the tawaf an elderly man whom worship had exhausted, his color turned yellow, with a staff in his hand, circling the House while leaning on it. I approached him and began to ask him. He said to me, 'Where are you from?' I said, 'From Khurasan.' He said, 'In what region is Khurasan?' as if he did not know it. I said, 'A region of the eastern lands.' He said, 'How long do you take to cover this journey?' I said, 'Two or three months.' He said, 'Do you not perform Hajj every year, since you are neighbors of this House?' I said to him, 'And how far is it between you and this House?' He said, 'A five-year journey. I left my land when there was no white in my head or beard.' I said, 'By Allah, this is a manifest exertion, a beautiful obedience, and a true love.' He smiled in my face and recited:

Visit the one you love, even if the home is far away
and between you and him are veils and curtains.
Distance should not prevent you from visiting him,
for the lover is always a visitor to the one he desires.
[Al-'Uhud al-Muhammadiyya – al-Sha'rani: 437.]

﴿That they may witness﴾: that they may be present. ﴿Benefits for them﴾: meaning trade. This is from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and it is the narration of Ibn Ruzayn from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: they are the markets.

Mujahid: trade, and what pleases Allah, glorified is He, of the affairs of this world and the Hereafter.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, 'Ata' al-'Awfi, and Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir: pardon and forgiveness.

﴿And mention the name of Allah on known days﴾: meaning the days of Dhu al-Hijjah according to the view of most exegetes. The ﴿counted days﴾ are the days of tashriq (the days after 'Id al-Adha). They were called "counted" (ma'dudat) because they are few. It was said that the ten days are called "known" (ma'lumat) out of eagerness to know them by reckoning, because the time of Hajj is at their end.

Muqatil said: "The known days are the days of tashriq."

Muhammad ibn Ka'b: "The counted and the known are one and the same."

﴿Over what He has provided for them from the cattle of livestock﴾: meaning the offerings (hada') and sacrificial animals (dahaya) of camels, cows, and sheep.

﴿So eat from them﴾: an imperative of permission, not obligation. The exegetes said: He said this because the people of jahiliyyah used to slaughter their offerings and would not eat anything from the meat of their offerings.

﴿And feed the miserable one﴾: meaning the one afflicted (zamin), the poor one who has nothing. ﴿Then let them complete their (state of) unkemptness﴾ (thumma li-yaqdu): the readers differed on these lam's. Some pronounced them with a kasrah to distinguish thumma from waw and fa', and al-Farra' did so because thumma is a separated part of speech, while waw and fa' are like part of the same word. Others pronounced them with a sukun because they are all lam of command. ﴿Their unkemptness (tafath)﴾: "tafath" means:

All the rites of Hajj, according to Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Qurazi and Mujahid said: it is the rites of Hajj, trimming the mustache, plucking the armpit hair, shaving the pubic hair, and cutting the nails.

'Ikrimah: tafath is hair and nails.

Al-Walibi, from Ibn 'Abbas: it is removing the state of ihram: shaving the head, cutting the nails, wearing clothes, and similar things. The original meaning of tafath in the language is filth. The Arabs say to a man whom they find disgusting, "How dirty you are (ma atfathaka)!" meaning, "How filthy you are! How repulsive you are!" Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

Their armpits were clean; they had not been soiled by filth,
and they had removed from themselves lice and nits.
[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 12/50.]

﴿And let them fulfill their vows﴾: Mujahid said: the vow of Hajj and of the offering, and whatever a person vows of something that is part of the Hajj.

﴿And let them circumambulate the Ancient House﴾: meaning the obligatory tawaf, which is the tawaf al-ifadah (the tawaf of return or visitation), performed after the 'Arafat stay, whether on the day of sacrifice or after it. The scholars differed on the meaning of "ancient" (atiq). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, and Qatadah said: it was called ancient because Allah, glorified is He, freed it (a'taqahu) from tyrants who would reach to destroy it. No tyrant ever overpowered it, and no one was empowered over it except those who would venerate and respect it.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Tubba' came intending to demolish the House. When he reached Qudayd, he was struck with paralysis. He called the rabbis, and they said: "This House has a Lord. No one who intends evil toward it is spared from being struck with harm by Him. If you want to be saved from what has befallen you, do not approach it with evil." He said: So he sent a gift to the House, a covering and leather hides, and it was the first thing to be covered. He slaughtered a thousand camels there, pardoned his people, honored them, and kept ties with them. Thus the place was called al-Matabikh (the kitchens) for the cooking of the people; his horses were excellent, so it was named Jiyad for the horses of Tubba'; and Qu'ayqi'an was named for the clatter of weapons when he came from Madinah.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: It was named so because it was never owned (lam yumlak qatt). This is also the narration of 'Ubayd from Mujahid, who said: "The House was named 'ancient' only because no one has any possession in it."

Ibn Zayd said: because it is ancient, and it is the first house placed for the people. It is said: a sword that is atiq (old) or a dinar that is atiq, meaning old. It was also said: because it is noble before Allah, glorified is He. The Arabs say: a horse that is atiq (noble).

﴿That (is so). And whoever honors the sacred rites of Allah﴾, by avoiding His disobedience, ﴿it is better for him in the sight of his Lord﴾.

Ibn Zayd said: The sacred things (hurumat) are al-Mash'ar al-Haram, the Sacred House, the Sacred Mosque, and the Sacred City. It was also said: they are the rites (manasik).

﴿And lawful to you are the cattle (an'am)﴾ to eat when you have slaughtered them, ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ in the Qur'an, which is His saying: ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion and blood﴾ [5:3] to the end of the verse, and His saying: ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾ [6:121]. It was also said: ﴿And lawful to you are the cattle﴾ during your state of ihram, ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ concerning game, for it is forbidden during the state of ihram.

﴿So avoid the filth of idols﴾: meaning worshipping them, because all idols are filth.

﴿And avoid the speech of falsehood﴾: meaning lying and slander.

Ayman ibn Hurrayn said: The Prophet (ﷺ) gave a sermon and said: "O people! The false testimony has been made equal to associating partners with Allah," then he recited this verse. [5] [Musnad Ahmad: 4/178.]

Some of them said: it is the statement of the polytheists in their talbiyah: "Here I am, You have no partner, except a partner who is Yours; You own him and what he owns."

﴿Ḥunafa'﴾: upright, sincere, devoted to Allah. It was also said: pilgrims. ﴿Not associating anything with Him﴾. ﴿And whoever associates with Allah, it is as if he had fallen from the sky﴾, meaning he dropped to the earth, ﴿and the birds snatch him away﴾. The words khatf and ikhtitaf mean taking something swiftly. The people of Madinah read ﴿fatakhattafuhu﴾ with a fatha on the kha' and shaddah on the ta', meaning tatakhattafuhu, and they assimilated the letters. The reading of the general readers is confirmed by His saying: ﴿except one who snatches a snatch﴾ [37:10].

﴿Or the wind carries him off to a distant place﴾: meaning far away.

The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: The condition of the polytheist is compared to that of one who falls, in that he possesses no benefit for himself and no removal of harm on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Hasan said: The deeds of the disbelievers are compared to this state, in that they are swept away and nullified, so they are unable to achieve anything from them.

﴿That (is so)﴾, meaning what I have mentioned of avoiding filth and falsehood and glorifying the rites of Allah, ﴿is from the piety of hearts﴾. This is the meaning and arrangement of the verse. The rites of Allah (sha'a'ir Allah) are the offerings (hady) and the camels (budn). The root is from ish'ar (marking), which is announcing them so that they may be recognized as offerings, and they are named after it. Glorifying them means deeming them great, finding them beautiful, and choosing them to be fat.

﴿For you in them﴾, meaning in the offerings, ﴿are benefits﴾. It was said: that their owner names them a budnah or hady, marks them, and garlands them, and you may benefit from their milk, wool, and fur, and ride upon their backs. ﴿Until a specified term﴾: which is that once he names it an offering and makes it obligatory, then when he does so, he has no benefit from them. Al-Akhfash: the humbled. Ibn Jarir: the submissive. 'Amr ibn Aws: those who do not wrong, and if they are wronged, they do not seek retribution.

﴿Standing in rows (sawaff)﴾: meaning standing on three legs, with their feet arranged and one of their forelegs bound, and the left foreleg tied, so the animal is slaughtered in that position.

Mujahid said: "Sawaff" means when its left hind leg is tied, and it stands on three legs, and it is slaughtered in that manner.

﴿Thus We have subjected them to you, that you may be grateful﴾.
